### Full-Time Supervision: Design Intent Verification

Full-Time Supervision services focus on quality control and design verification throughout construction. Supervisors ensure that materials, workmanship, and methods conform to design specifications and technical standards. Authority remains limited to technical matters within the design scope. Supervisors verify contractor compliance without managing overall project coordination or cost control. This service emphasizes architectural expertise in evaluating construction quality against design intent.

### Construction Management: Project Delivery Coordination

Construction Management services encompass broader project coordination beyond quality verification. Construction managers address schedule progression, cost control, multi-trade coordination, and resource management. Authority extends to business decisions affecting project delivery including contractor scheduling, cost management, and change order processing. Construction managers function as owner representatives managing relationships among all project participants. This service emphasizes project management expertise and business acumen alongside technical knowledge.

### SPP 202 Regular Design Services: Comprehensive Engagement Model

SPP 202 Design Administration establishes the architect's involvement from concept through occupancy. Regular design services encompass project definition, schematic design, design development, contract documents, bidding/negotiation, and construction phases. Supervisory functions form one component of comprehensive design administration. Administration services may include design development consultation, construction issue resolution, and building operation guidance beyond supervision alone. This integrated model maintains architect involvement across all project phases.

### Key Functional Differences

Supervision focuses exclusively on design compliance verification during construction. Construction management adds business coordination, cost control, and stakeholder management. Design administration integrates design decisions with construction execution and post-occupancy support. These distinctions establish different professional relationships, authority scopes, and compensation methods. Project requirements and owner preferences determine which service model best suits specific engagements.

### Compensation Method Distinctions

Full-time supervision typically employs percentage of construction cost or fixed fees based on hours and site presence. Construction management uses percentage, hourly, or performance-based methods reflecting broader responsibility scope. Design administration encompasses fees for entire project delivery from concept through occupancy. Compensation methods align with service scope and professional responsibility intensity. Clear fee structures prevent disputes and establish mutual understanding of value exchange.

### Legal Responsibility and Liability

Supervisors bear professional responsibility for identifying non-conformance and recommending correction. Construction managers assume coordination accuracy and cost control responsibilities within their authority scope. Design administrators maintain continuous professional involvement throughout project delivery. Article 1723 of the Civil Code imposes liability on the contractor and the architect/engineer who directed the structural work if it fails due to defects in materials or workmanship. Limitation of authority agreements protect professionals when operating within defined scope.

## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- State the four-tiered hierarchy of ethical obligations: Public, Client, Profession, Fellow Architects.
- Explain why public welfare always takes precedence over client interests.
- Identify SPP Document 200 as the Code of Ethical Conduct.
- Distinguish ethical obligations (SPP 200) from standards of practice (SPP 201–209).

SPP Document 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct) defines the architect's ethical obligations to four distinct stakeholders in ranked order: Public, Client, Profession, and Fellow Architects. RA 9266, signed June 18, 2004, mandates compliance with this Code and establishes the PRBoA as the 3-member enforcement body.

## Core Concept

The Code of Ethical Conduct (SPP Document 200) is the mandatory framework governing architect behavior in the Philippines under RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004). The code does not prescribe service delivery methods but establishes moral and professional obligations. It differs from Standards of Professional Practice documents 201-209, which specify how to deliver services.

Breach of these obligations creates grounds for professional sanctions, suspension, or license revocation.

| Disclose conflicts of interest; refuse hidden compensation | Section 2-i, 4-b | Tests whether architect can accept material discounts from suppliers |

| Do not assume commission being negotiated by another architect | Section 5-c, 5-e | Tests whether notification requirement applies to known prior engagement |
| PRBoA = 1 Chairman + 2 Members (3-member board) | RA 9266 Section 4 | Tests board composition understanding |
| Grounds for discipline in Section 23 | Section 23 | Tests sanctions for specific violations (signing unsealed work, false claims) |
| IAPOA (Integrated and Accredited Professional Organization of Architects) = UAP | RA 9266 Sec 40 & 41 | Tests equivalent terminology and professional organization authority |

## Philippine Practice Context

The Code of Ethical Conduct is enforceable law under RA 9266, not advisory guidance. Architects in the Philippines practice under a singular code that applies equally to all licensed professionals regardless of firm size or project type. The PRBoA investigates complaints and imposes discipline through the PRC structure. Compliance is non-negotiable for license renewal and liability protection. The code's emphasis on public welfare before client interest reflects the profession's societal role in safeguarding built environment safety and accessibility.

## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Lea Prac Eth 010 Introduction** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?
## Introduction
## Learning Goal
After reading this article, you should understand the key concepts tested in the LEA for this topic, including relevant code provisions, dimensional standards, and common exam applications.

The LEA examination tests candidates' ability to recognize unprofessional conduct in realistic scenarios. Rather than abstract ethical rules, architects must identify violations in context—understanding when conduct crosses from acceptable professional practice into violation territory.

This article presents a taxonomy of unprofessional conduct patterns based on RA 9266 Section 23 (grounds for suspension/revocation), the Code of Ethical Conduct, and Standards of Professional Practice. Each pattern is illustrated with scenarios showing how violations manifest in practice and what disciplinary consequences follow.

## The Conduct Spectrum

Not all poor professional judgment constitutes disciplinary violation. The conduct spectrum ranges from:

```
Acceptable Practice → Gray Area → Professional Deviation → Violation
```

**Acceptable Practice:** Actions within professional discretion, consistent with standards

Each cell shows representative scenarios. Bottom section shows the four-step mandatory process: Recognize → Disclose → Obtain Informed Consent → Recuse if irreconcilable.", placementIntent="conflict-resolution", suggestedSearchQuery="architect conflict of interest matrix type severity disclosure recusal Code of Ethics", suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image"

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]
**Gray Area:** Practices that may be questionable but have professional defenders
**Professional Deviation:** Breach of clear standard but not egregious
**Violation:** Clear breach that justifies discipline
```

Understanding this spectrum is critical because LEA scenarios ask candidates to distinguish between actions that are poor judgment versus actions that constitute violations.

## Pattern 1: Negligence and Failure to Meet Standard of Care

<ExamTip />

<Warn />

<LawCallout />

### Definition

Negligence in architecture occurs when an architect fails to exercise the reasonable care and skill that a competent architect in similar circumstances would exercise. It involves:

- **Deviation from applicable standards** (codes, best practices, professional norms)
- **Failure to perform required services** or perform them inadequately
- **Breach of professional duty** owed to client, public, or other parties
- **Causation of harm or loss** as a result

### Negligence Categories

<ComparisonTable />

### Scenario 1: Design Negligence

**Situation:** Architect Raj designs an office building with floor slabs calculated for standard office loads (2.5 kPa live load) without inquiry into tenant use. The building is later leased to a data center operator requiring 5 kPa loads. The increased loading causes deflection and cracking.

**Analysis:**
- **Negligent element:** Failed to investigate or confirm intended use before design
- **Violated standard:** Professional practice requires investigating client needs and intended use
- **Causation:** The under-designed slabs directly caused structural distress
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 2-3 years; restitution for repair costs

<ExamTip />

### Scenario 2: Construction Administration Negligence

**Situation:** Architect Carmen conducts monthly site inspections but the general contractor installs exterior walls with inadequate flashing details that are not in accordance with the approved drawings. Carmen's inspection photos show the defective work, but she files no non-compliance notice and does not require remediation.

**Analysis:**
- **Negligent element:** Observed code violation but failed to enforce correction
- **Violated standard:** Architect's duty during construction admin is to verify compliance
- **Causation:** Water infiltration and interior damage result from uncorrected defect
- **Likely discipline:** Probation 1-2 years; requirement to complete CA training

**Key distinction:** Carmen observed the defect (she has knowledge), making her failure to act more culpable than if she had unknowingly missed it.

### Scenario 3: Site Investigation Negligence

**Situation:** Architect Dakota designs a building foundation on a hillside without conducting a geotechnical investigation or consulting with a geotechnical engineer. Subsequent construction reveals unstable soil conditions requiring expensive foundation modifications.

**Analysis:**
- **Negligent element:** Failed to investigate site conditions before foundation design
- **Violated standard:** Professional practice requires competent site investigation
- **Causation:** Inadequate investigation led directly to foundation design errors
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 2-3 years; liability for modification costs

<LeartBox />

## Pattern 2: Incompetence and Lack of Professional Qualifications

### Definition

Incompetence differs from negligence: an architect may lack the skill or knowledge to perform required services, even with care. It includes:

- **Practicing outside scope of expertise**
- **Lacking specialized knowledge required for the project type**
- **Failing to consult specialists when needed**
- **Misrepresenting qualifications or experience**

### Incompetence Scenarios

**Scenario 4: Scope Overreach**

**Situation:** Architect Evan, specializing in residential design, accepts a commission to design a complex underground parking structure without structural engineering expertise and without employing a structural engineer. The design is later found to violate code for underground facilities.

**Analysis:**
- **Incompetence element:** Lacked expertise for specialized project type
- **Violated standard:** Must employ qualified specialists or decline services outside expertise
- **Causation:** Lack of structural competence led to code violation
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 2-3 years; mandatory specialist consultation requirement

**Scenario 5: Misrepresented Qualifications**

**Situation:** Architect Fiona applies for a government project requiring 10 years of healthcare facility design experience. She submits a resume showing healthcare projects, but omits that she only performed junior designer roles under supervision. The awarded design later has inadequate infection control provisions.

**Analysis:**
- **Incompetence and fraud:** Misrepresented qualification level and lacked independent expertise
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics requires honest representation of qualifications
- **Causation:** Represented expertise she did not possess; design deficiency resulted
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 3-5 years; possible revocation if pattern of misrepresentation

<ExamTip />

## Pattern 3: Dishonesty and Fraudulent Conduct

### Definition

Dishonesty includes deliberate falsification, fraud, and deception, including:

- **Falsifying documents** (design certifications, compliance statements)
- **Fraudulent billing** (charging for services not rendered; inflating hours)
- **Misrepresenting design compliance** (certifying non-compliant work as compliant)
- **Forging signatures or stamps**
- **False statements to clients, contractors, or authorities**

### Dishonesty Scenarios

**Scenario 6: Certification Fraud**

**Situation:** Architect Greta, under time pressure, certifies that a building design complies with the Philippine Building Code without actually performing the compliance review. Subsequent construction reveals multiple code violations (inadequate fire-rated exits, non-compliant stair dimensions).

**Analysis:**
- **Fraudulent element:** Signed compliance certification knowing it was false
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics Section 1 requires honesty and integrity; RA 9266 requires truthful certifications
- **Causation:** False certification allowed non-compliant design to proceed
- **Harm:** Public safety risk; life safety code violations
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 3-5 years; possible revocation (fraud with safety consequences)

<LeartBox />

**Scenario 7: Billing Fraud**

**Situation:** Architect Hector bills a client for design services on a luxury residence including 200 hours of "structural analysis." In reality, he outsourced the structural design to an engineer for $5,000 and invoiced the client for 200 hours at $150/hour ($30,000), pocketing $25,000 profit.

**Analysis:**
- **Fraudulent element:** Misrepresented services provided and charged inflated hours
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics requires honest dealing with clients
- **Causation:** Client paid significantly more than fair value for work
- **Restitution:** Client entitled to refund of unjust enrichment
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 2-3 years; mandatory restitution; ethics training

**Scenario 8: Document Forgery**

**Situation:** Architect Ivan, needing to show a building design complying with setback requirements, creates a forged municipal zoning certification indicating the lot qualifies for a setback variance. He submits this to the client as authentic.

**Analysis:**
- **Fraudulent element:** Created false government document
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics Section 1 (honesty); RA 9266 Section 23(c) (fraudulent conduct)
- **Legal consequences:** May also constitute criminal forgery
- **Harm:** Client relies on false document; potential exposure to liability
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 3-5 years minimum; likely revocation if involving government documents

## Pattern 4: Conflicts of Interest and Self-Dealing

### Definition

Conflicts of interest occur when an architect has competing financial or professional interests that compromise objectivity, including:

- **Undisclosed financial interests in contractors or suppliers**
- **Accepting commissions from building material suppliers without disclosure**
- **Serving multiple parties with opposing interests (client and contractor) without disclosure**
- **Self-dealing** (profiting from services recommended to client)
- **Nepotism and favoritism** in hiring or contracting

### Conflicts of Interest Scenarios

**Scenario 9: Undisclosed Supplier Interest**

**Situation:** Architect Jake receives a 15% commission from a curtain wall supplier for every project he specifies their systems. He does not disclose this financial arrangement to clients. When selecting curtain wall systems for projects, he consistently specifies the supplier's high-cost products even when equivalent lower-cost alternatives exist.

**Analysis:**
- **Conflict element:** Financial interest in supplier clouds judgment
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics requires full disclosure of conflicts; architect must act in client's best interest
- **Causation:** Clients overpay for curtain wall systems due to specification bias
- **Client harm:** Unnecessary cost increase
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 1-2 years; mandatory restitution of commissions; disclosure requirement for future

<ExamTip />

**Scenario 10: Undisclosed Multiple Representation**

**Situation:** Architect Kate agrees to design a commercial building for a client (the developer). Simultaneously, without the developer's knowledge, she agrees to design the general contractor's temporary site facilities for the same project. The contractor's facilities plan requires extra site area, conflicting with the developer's space plan.

**Analysis:**
- **Conflict element:** Competing interests of developer and contractor without either knowing
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics requires exclusive loyalty and full disclosure
- **Harm:** Developer's design interests compromised; contractor given undue influence
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 1-3 years; loss of both client relationships; restitution

**Scenario 11: Accepting Kickbacks from Suppliers**

**Situation:** Architect Leo accepts cash "gifts" from a structural engineering firm in exchange for directing projects to them for subconsultant work. The gifts are disguised as "professional development contributions." Over three years, Leo receives $50,000 in hidden payments.

**Analysis:**
- **Conflict element:** Financial incentive to recommend firms regardless of merit
- **Fraud element:** Disguised payments constitute concealed kickbacks
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics Section 4 (honest professional relationships)
- **Potential harm:** Clients may not receive services from best-qualified subconsultants
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 3-5 years; possible revocation; mandatory restitution; potential criminal prosecution

## Pattern 5: Breach of Fiduciary Duty to Client

### Definition

Architects owe clients a fiduciary duty requiring them to:

- **Prioritize client interests over personal interests**
- **Guard client confidential information**
- **Account for client funds and payments**
- **Avoid abandoning client without cause**
- **Provide competent advice and services**

### Fiduciary Breach Scenarios

**Scenario 12: Abandonment of Client**

**Situation:** Architect Martin accepts a commission to design a hospital addition. He completes schematic design and receives partial payment. Midway through design development, a more lucrative project opportunity appears. Martin informs the client he is "unable to continue" without explanation and does not facilitate transition to another architect.

**Analysis:**
- **Breach element:** Abandoned client project without legitimate cause or proper transition
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics requires completing services or ensuring proper successor
- **Causation:** Client incurs costs and delays finding replacement architect
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 1-2 years; mandatory restitution of unearned fee; ethics training

<LeartBox />

**Scenario 13: Failure to Return Client Documents**

**Situation:** Architect Nora completes a project and receives final payment. The client requests return of all design documents, survey data, and geotechnical reports. Nora retains the documents, claiming they are "her work product" and potential future reference.

**Analysis:**
- **Breach element:** Client-provided information belongs to client and must be returned
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics; professional contract terms (typically require return upon request)
- **Causation:** Client cannot fully utilize building for future modifications or operations
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 1-2 years; mandatory document return; restitution if client harm demonstrated

**Scenario 14: Commingling and Misuse of Client Funds**

**Situation:** Architect Oscar receives $200,000 in advance payment from a client for design services. He deposits this into his general operating account (not a trust account) and uses $50,000 for office renovation. The remaining funds are eventually returned to the client when the project is completed, but for 6 months the client's funds were used for Oscar's business purposes.

**Analysis:**
- **Fiduciary breach:** Client funds misused; not held in separate trust account
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics requires segregation of client funds; professional standards require trust accounting
- **Causation:** Client's funds used for architect's purposes; risk of loss if business failed
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 2-3 years; mandatory restitution of interest; mandatory trust accounting training; possible criminal prosecution if deliberate theft

## Pattern 6: Unprofessional Conduct and Unfit Character

### Definition

Beyond specific violations, RA 9266 Section 23(g) authorizes discipline for "any other act or conduct which is prejudicial to the best interest of the public or the integrity of the profession." This includes:

- **Criminal conviction** (felony or crime of moral turpitude)
- **Habitual intoxication or substance abuse** affecting practice
- **Harassment, discrimination, or bullying** of colleagues or staff
- **Violation of court orders or regulatory directives**
- **Gross violation of building codes** or safety standards

### Unfit Character Scenarios

**Scenario 15: Criminal Conviction**

**Situation:** Architect Paul is convicted of felony tax evasion for underreporting income from his architecture practice over five years. He receives a sentence of 2 years in federal prison.

**Analysis:**
- **Unfit character element:** Criminal conviction indicates dishonesty and poor character judgment
- **Violated standard:** RA 9266 Section 23 allows discipline for criminal conviction involving moral turpitude
- **Public trust breach:** Licensure carries expectation of trustworthiness and lawfulness
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension during incarceration; possible revocation upon conviction depending on sentencing and severity

<ExamTip />

**Scenario 16: Habitual Substance Abuse**

**Situation:** Architect Quinn demonstrates a pattern of substance abuse affecting professional judgment. During a site inspection, he appears impaired, makes unsafe decisions regarding an open excavation, and nearly causes an accident. Multiple staff members report concerns about his behavior.

**Analysis:**
- **Unfit character element:** Substance abuse compromises professional judgment and endangers safety
- **Violated standard:** RA 9266 Section 23(g); Code of Ethics Section 1 (fitness to practice)
- **Public safety risk:** Impaired decision-making during construction administration
- **Likely discipline:** Mandatory suspension until completion of treatment program; possible revocation if no successful rehabilitation; reinstatement conditioned on ongoing monitoring

**Scenario 17: Harassment of Subordinates**

**Situation:** Architect Rosa creates a hostile work environment through verbal abuse, discriminatory comments toward junior female staff, and public humiliation of staff members who make minor errors. Multiple staff members file complaints.

**Analysis:**
- **Unfit character element:** Harassment and discrimination violate professional conduct standards
- **Violated standard:** Code of Ethics Section 6 (responsibilities to subordinates); anti-discrimination laws
- **Causation:** Staff harm; negative professional environment; potential legal liability
- **Likely discipline:** Suspension 1-2 years; mandatory ethics and management training; restitution to harmed staff if settlement required

## Pattern 7: Violation of Regulatory Requirements and Court Orders

### Definition

Professional discipline is also imposed for:

- **Practicing without current license** or with expired registration
- **Violating PRBoA or PRC directives** (e.g., orders to cease certain practices)
- **Failing to maintain continuing professional development** requirements
- **Non-compliance with statutory reporting** (e.g., failure to report discipline of other licensees)
- **Violation of court orders** (e.g., orders from litigation)

### Regulatory Violation Scenarios

**Scenario 18: Practicing Without Current License**

**Situation:** Architect Sam's license expires on December 31, 2025. He fails to renew and continues accepting and executing architectural commissions into January 2026 without current license. He later renews the license in February 2026 after a client complaint.

**Analysis:**
- **Violation element:** Practiced architecture without current license
- **Violated standard:** RA 9266 Section 34 requires current license for practice
- **Harm:** Client services performed by unlicensed "architect"; public protection compromised
- **Likely discipline:** Probation 1-2 years; fine; requirement to notify clients of unlicensed period

**Scenario 19: Failing to Comply with PRBoA Directive**

**Situation:** Following a PRBoA decision directing Architect Tina to obtain mentoring from a senior architect in structural design, Tina ignores the directive and continues independent structural design work without mentoring. She later faces a new complaint for inadequate structural design.

**Analysis:**
- **Violation element:** Willfully violated PRBoA compliance order
- **Violated standard:** RA 9266 Section 37 (PRBoA authority); professional obligation to comply with regulatory directives
- **Aggravating factor:** Demonstrated disrespect for regulatory authority; pattern of structural design problems
- **Likely discipline:** Enhanced penalty for previous violation; suspension 2-3 years; mandatory compliance monitoring

## Conduct Severity Framework

Not all violations are equally serious. The PRBoA applies a severity framework:

<ComparisonTable />

## Mitigating and Aggravating Factors

The PRBoA considers factors beyond the violation itself:

### Mitigating Factors (Supporting Lighter Discipline)

- **First offense** by previously unblemished architect
- **Good faith effort** to comply or remedy
- **Client satisfaction** despite error
- **Prompt correction** of defect when identified
- **Genuine remorse** and commitment to improvement
- **Completion of remedial training** proactively
- **Difficult project circumstances** (unusually constrained timeline, etc.)

### Aggravating Factors (Supporting Harsher Discipline)

- **Pattern of violations** (repeat offender)
- **Deliberate conduct** (versus inadvertent error)
- **Concealment** of violation or dishonesty about it
- **Significant harm** resulting from violation
- **Public safety consequences**
- **Abuse of professional position** or client trust
- **Violation while under prior discipline** or regulatory order

<ExamTip />

## The Role of Intent and Negligence Versus Fraud

A critical LEA distinction: **did the architect intend the violation or act negligently?**

- **Negligent violation:** Architect exercised care but fell short of standard; often deserves probation/suspended sentence
- **Reckless violation:** Architect was indifferent to whether standard was met; typically deserves suspension
- **Intentional/fraudulent violation:** Architect deliberately violated standard or deceived; typically deserves revocation

**Scenario 20: Distinguishing Intent Levels**

Three architects all failed to perform site investigation before foundation design:

**Architect A:** Relied on client representation that site had been investigated; did not know investigation was inadequate (negligent—deserves probation)

**Architect B:** Knew site investigation was needed but skipped it due to budget constraints; hoped for the best (reckless—deserves suspension)

**Architect C:** Knew site investigation was needed and deliberately didn't perform it, then falsely certified the design was based on proper investigation (fraudulent—deserves revocation)

Same violation (inadequate site investigation) yields vastly different discipline based on architect's mental state.

## Summary Table: Violation Patterns and Likely Discipline

<ComparisonTable />

## About This Article

This article is part of the SlateCamp Professional Practice Content Engine for LEA preparation. It synthesizes regulatory frameworks, case law principles, and professional standards into competency-based learning outcomes aligned with the Licensure Examination for Architects syllabus.

# Building Permit Process


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Building Permit Process** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?
## Learning Goal
After reading this article, you should be able to:

Explain the complete building permit process under PD 1096 Rule III: identify the Building Official's powers and duties, apply the 15-day payment-to-decision rule, determine when permits expire (1 year / 120 days), and distinguish exempt constructions from those requiring full permits or accessory permits.
---

## Schema Activation: Two Projects, Two Different Worlds

You are the lead architect on two simultaneous projects:

1. A new public library in Quezon City — a government-funded building costing P50 million.
2. A traditional bamboo house for your uncle in Ifugao — native materials, family use only, total cost P12,000.

Which one pays building permit fees? Which one needs a permit at all? Who enforces compliance on both?

If you cannot answer these instantly, this module is exactly what you need.

---

## Part 1: The Building Official (OBO)

### Who Is the Building Official?

The **Building Official (BO)** is the duly appointed government authority at the local level — typically the City or Municipal Engineer — responsible for carrying out the provisions of PD 1096 within their jurisdiction.

**Reason for the Law:** A single, identifiable local authority creates clear accountability. If a permitted building collapses, there is no ambiguity about which office reviewed and approved the plans.

### Powers and Duties (Rule II, Sec. 205-207, Revised IRR)

| Function            | What the Building Official Does                                                                                                        |
| :------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Plan Review**     | Examines submitted drawings, specifications, and documents for compliance with the National Building Code and all referenced standards |
| **Permit Issuance** | Issues building permits, ancillary permits, and certificates of occupancy when compliance is demonstrated                              |
| **Site Inspection** | Conducts inspections at critical construction phases to verify that actual work matches approved plans                                 |
| **Enforcement**     | Issues work stoppage orders, demolition orders, and imposes administrative fines for violations                                        |
| **Fee Collection**  | Collects building permit fees and surcharges on behalf of the local government                                                         |

**Reason for the Law:** Concentrated authority prevents fragmentation. Without a single enforcement officer, contractors and owners could exploit gaps between agencies to bypass safety requirements.

| **Denial requirement**           | Must be **in writing**, citing specific Code provisions, within the same 15-day window                                         |

### Permit Validity and Expiration (Sec. 305, PD 1096 / Rule III, Sec. 305, Revised IRR)

A building permit becomes **null and void** if either condition below occurs:

| Expiration Trigger                   | Threshold                                                                                           |
| :----------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Failure to commence construction** | Construction has not begun within **one (1) year** from the date of permit issuance                 |
| **Abandonment after commencement**   | Construction is suspended or abandoned for a continuous period of **120 days** after work has begun |

**Reason for the Law:** Permits are not licenses to build indefinitely. The one-year commencement rule prevents landowners from hoarding approved permits for speculative purposes. The 120-day abandonment rule ensures that half-built structures — which are hazardous — cannot be left open-ended.

Extracted summary:
- Props: code="pd1096", section="Rule I - Section 106 - Permit Application"
- Text: The Two Clocks That Kill Your Permit:
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]
>
> - **1 year** to START
> - **120 days** to NOT STOP

## Part 3: Exemptions — The Most-Tested LEA Topic in This Module

There are two entirely separate categories of exemption. Confusing them is the most common error on the board exam.

| Category             | What Is Waived                  | What Is NOT Waived                                 | Legal Basis             |
| :------------------- | :------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------- |
| **Fee Exemption**    | Payment of building permit fees | The building permit itself — still required        | Sec. 209, PD 1096       |
| **Permit Exemption** | The building permit itself      | Nothing — structure may still not violate the Code | Sec. 301.3, Revised IRR |

---

### Fee Exemptions (Sec. 209, PD 1096)

These two categories of structures must still obtain a building permit and submit plans for safety review. They are only excused from **paying** the fees.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — FEE EXEMPTION TABLE**

| Exempt Category                             | All Conditions Required                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Reason for the Law                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| :------------------------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Public Buildings**                        | Government-owned; funded by the national or local government (e.g., public schools, city halls, state universities, public hospitals)                                                                                                                       | The government cannot charge itself permit fees paid from the same public funds. The fee would be circular. Safety review, however, still applies in full — a government building must meet the same standards as private construction. |
| **Traditional Indigenous Family Dwellings** | (1) Intended for use and occupancy by the **family of the owner only** — no rental, no commercial use; (2) Constructed of **native materials** (bamboo, nipa, logs, or lumber from the site); (3) Total cost of construction does **not exceed P15,000.00** | Imposing permit fees on a P12,000 bamboo home would represent a disproportionate financial burden on low-income rural families. The P15,000 threshold is the line below which fee collection is considered inequitable.                 |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Note" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: Critical Note: Both of these structures still undergo the full permit review process. A government building's plans are reviewed for structural safety, fire safety, and sanitation just like any private project. Only the payment of fees is waived.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

> **Exam Caveat — Traditional Indigenous Family Dwellings**  
> PD 1096 Sec. 209 states that **public buildings and traditional indigenous family dwellings are exempt only from payment of building permit fees**, not from the permit requirement itself. Some review materials and local practices say that traditional indigenous family dwellings are entirely outside the Code and treat them as **permit‑exempt**. For this module (and for LEA safety), we follow the **stricter Code‑text reading**: permit still required, fees waived. Always match your answer to the exact wording of the exam question.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — TRAP #2: "No Fee" Does NOT Mean "No Permit"**

|                                         | Wrong                                       | Right                                                          |
| :-------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A public school building...             | Does not need a building permit             | Needs a full building permit — only **fee-exempt** (Sec. 209)  |
| A bamboo family home costing P12,000... | Is exempt from both the permit and the fees | Needs a building permit — only **fee-exempt** (Sec. 209)       |
| **What is actually permit-exempt?**     | Anything over 6 sq.m                        | Specific minor constructions under Sec. 301.3, IRR — see below |

---

### Permit Exemptions (Rule III, Sec. 301.3, Revised IRR of PD 1096)

These structures and works do **not require a building permit** — provided they do not violate any other provision of the Code (zoning, setbacks, easements, etc.).

#### A. Minor Constructions

| Type of Structure                                                                                                          | Maximum Dimension or Condition                                                                                                                   |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Sheds, outhouses, greenhouses, children's playhouses, aviaries, poultry houses, and similar structures                     | Not exceeding **6.00 sq.m.** in total floor area; must be **completely detached** from any other building; for **private use of the owner only** |
| Open terraces or patios resting directly on the ground                                                                     | Not exceeding **20.00 sq.m.** in total floor area; for **private use of the owner only**                                                         |
| Window grilles                                                                                                             | Installation only (no size threshold stated in the IRR)                                                                                          |
| Garden pools for water plants or aquarium fish                                                                             | Not exceeding **500 mm** in depth; for **private use only**                                                                                      |
| **Garden masonry walls** (other than party walls); also includes garden footpaths, residential garden walks, and driveways | Not exceeding **1.20 meters** in height                                                                                                          |

**Reason for the Law:** A 5 sq.m. garden shed poses negligible structural and life-safety risk. Requiring a full building permit for every garden tool enclosure would paralyze the OBO with trivial applications and discourage routine property upkeep. The thresholds are calibrated to the point where structural complexity and public safety risk become meaningful.

#### B. Repair Works

All of the following are exempt **only if** they do not affect or involve any structural member (beams, columns, load-bearing walls, foundations):

| Exempt Repair Work                                                                                      | Additional Condition                                |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :-------------------------------------------------- |
| Replacement of deteriorated roofing sheets or tiles, gutters, downspouts, fascias, ceilings, or sidings | Non-structural only                                 |
| Repair or replacement of non-load-bearing partition walls                                               | —                                                   |
| Repair or replacement of any interior portion of a house                                                | No addition or alteration of the structure involved |
| Repair or replacement of doors and windows                                                              | —                                                   |
| Repair or replacement of flooring                                                                       | —                                                   |
| Repair of perimeter fence and walls                                                                     | —                                                   |
| Repair or replacement of plumbing fixtures, fittings, or piping                                         | **Single detached dwellings and duplexes only**     |

**Reason for the Law:** Routine maintenance keeps buildings safe. If every gutter repair required a permit, owners would defer maintenance rather than face bureaucratic delays, resulting in more — not fewer — hazardous conditions. The structural-member boundary is the critical line: touching the structural skeleton requires engineering review and therefore a permit.

---

## Part 4: The Fence Rules — Three Thresholds, Zero Exceptions

> This is among the most frequently tested and most frequently confused topics in the LEA. There are three entirely distinct fence rules, each with its own legal basis.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — FENCE HEIGHT TABLE**

| Fence / Wall Type                          | Height                        | Permit Requirement                                                              | Legal Basis                      |
| :----------------------------------------- | :---------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :------------------------------- |
| **Garden masonry walls** (not party walls) | **1.20 m or below**           | **NO permit required** — exempt as minor construction                           | Sec. 301.3.a.v, Revised IRR      |
| **Standard fences** (any material)         | **Above 1.20 m up to 1.80 m** | **Accessory Permit only** — not a full Building Permit                          | Sec. 301.2.b.ii, Revised IRR     |
| **Tall fences**                            | **Above 1.80 m**              | **Full Building Permit required** — classified as Group J, Division 2 occupancy | Sec. 701 / Rule VII, Revised IRR |

**Reason for the Law:** A 1.0 m garden wall is decorative and structurally trivial. A 2.5 m masonry perimeter fence, by contrast, is a significant structure that can collapse onto pedestrians, retains soil loads, and affects neighboring properties. The graduated threshold ensures that meaningful structural risk triggers meaningful regulatory review.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — TRAP #3: "Under 1.80 m = No Permit" Is FALSE**

|                                    | Wrong                      | Right                                                                  |
| :--------------------------------- | :------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A 1.50 m perimeter fence...        | Is exempt from all permits | Requires an **Accessory Permit** (Sec. 301.2.b.ii)                     |
| A 1.10 m garden masonry wall...    | Needs an Accessory Permit  | Is **fully exempt** — no permit of any kind (Sec. 301.3.a.v)           |
| The 1.20 m threshold applies to... | All fences                 | **Garden masonry walls only** — not party walls, not structural fences |

## Part 5: Administrative Fines (Rule II, Sec. 212, Revised IRR of PD 1096)

The Secretary of the DPWH or an authorized representative may impose administrative fines for Code violations. These are civil penalties — they do not require criminal prosecution.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — ADMINISTRATIVE FINE TABLE**

| Violation Class | Fine Amount    | Representative Examples                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| :-------------- | :------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Light**       | **P5,000.00**  | Failure to post Certificate of Occupancy; failure to post the building permit construction information sign; failure to provide safety measures for workers, visitors, or pedestrians on the construction site                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Less Grave**  | **P8,000.00**  | Continuing construction work after a work stoppage order has been issued for alteration or repair without permit; use or occupancy of a building without a Certificate of Occupancy                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Grave**       | **P10,000.00** | Unauthorized change in submitted and approved plans; unauthorized change from more fire-resistive to less fire-resistive construction; non-compliance with a demolition order; non-compliance with a work stoppage order for construction or demolition without a permit; change in use or occupancy without a certificate; excavations left open for more than 120 days |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="tip", title="Mnemonic"
- Text: Administrative Fines: "5-8-10" Think of it as a fragmented phone number: **5 / 8 / 10**
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]
>
> - Light = **P5,000**
> - Less Grave = **P8,000**
> - Grave = **P10,000**

**Reason for the Law:** The graduated fine structure reflects proportionality. Missing a posted sign is a procedural lapse with minimal safety impact. Unauthorized structural changes or defying demolition orders directly endanger lives — those warrant the maximum administrative penalty. The three-tier system gives the OBO a proportionate enforcement toolkit.

---

## Part 6: Surcharges for Illegal Construction (Rule II, Sec. 212, Revised IRR)

Surcharges are **separate from and in addition to** administrative fines. They are calculated as a percentage of the **building permit fees** that would have been owed, and they escalate based on how far the illegal construction has progressed before discovery.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — SURCHARGE ESCALATOR TABLE**

| Stage of Illegal Construction When Discovered                        | Surcharge on Building Permit Fees |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------- |
| Excavation for foundation                                            | **10%**                           |
| Construction of foundation (including pile driving, rebar, formwork) | **25%**                           |
| Superstructure up to 2.00 m above established grade                  | **50%**                           |
| Superstructure **above 2.00 m** above established grade              | **100%**                          |

**Reason for the Law:** The surcharge escalator deters owners from continuing illegal construction after detection. The further you build without a permit, the more you pay — turning every additional meter of illegal construction into a compounding financial liability. Confiscating the equivalent of the full permit fee (100%) at the superstructure stage also eliminates any cost-savings rationale for skipping the permit.

---

## Part 7: Penal Sanctions — Criminal Liability (Sec. 213, PD 1096)

Penal sanctions are a completely separate enforcement track from administrative fines. They require formal criminal prosecution through the courts.

| Element                          | Detail                                                                                                                                    |
| :------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Maximum Criminal Fine**        | **Not more than P20,000.00**                                                                                                              |
| **Maximum Imprisonment**         | **Not more than 2 years**                                                                                                                 |
| **Application**                  | Fine **and/or** imprisonment — at the court's discretion based on the facts                                                               |
| **Corporate / Entity Liability** | If the violator is a corporation, firm, partnership, or association, the penalty falls on the **officials responsible** for the violation |
| **Alien Violators**              | Subject to immediate deportation after payment of the fine and/or service of the prison sentence                                          |

**Reason for the Law:** Administrative fines are fast and handled by the OBO, but they are capped at P10,000 and carry no freedom-limiting consequences. For willful, dangerous, and persistent Code violations, the legislature provided a criminal track with court-imposed sanctions — including imprisonment — as the ultimate deterrent.

---

**PATTERN INTERRUPT — TRAP #4: Administrative Fines vs. Penal Sanctions**

|                            | Administrative (Sec. 212, IRR)                    | Criminal / Penal (Sec. 213, PD 1096)                     |
| :------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Imposed by**             | Building Official / DPWH Secretary                | Court, after criminal prosecution                        |
| **Maximum fine**           | **P10,000.00** (Grave Violation)                  | **P20,000.00**                                           |
| **Imprisonment possible?** | No                                                | Yes — up to 2 years                                      |
| **Speed**                  | Administrative action — relatively fast           | Requires criminal prosecution — slow                     |
| **Common exam trap**       | Confusing P10,000 (admin) with P20,000 (criminal) | Assuming the P10,000 admin cap is the only possible fine |

## Quick-Fire Mnemonics

**"P.I.T." — Fee Exemption vs. Permit Exemption**

- **P**ublic buildings → fee-exempt (the government cannot charge itself)
- **I**ndigenous dwellings → fee-exempt (cost ≤ P15,000, native materials, family use only)
- **T**iny constructions → permit-exempt (≤ 6 sq.m. for sheds; specific thresholds for each type)

**Administrative Fines — "5-8-10"**

- Light = P**5**,000
- Less Grave = P**8**,000
- Grave = P**10**,000

**The Two Clocks That Kill Your Permit (Sec. 305)**

- **1 year** from issuance: must START construction
- **120 days** after starting: must NOT STOP construction

**Surcharge Escalator — "10-25-50-100"**

- Excavation = **10%**
- Foundation = **25%**
- Super ≤ 2.00 m = **50%**
- Super > 2.00 m = **100%**

**Penal Sanctions (Sec. 213) — "20-2"**

- Maximum fine: **P20,000**
- Maximum imprisonment: **2 years**
- These are criminal — courts only, not the OBO.

Read the facts carefully — examiners deliberately put both dates to test this specific distinction.

## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Lea Prac Law 001 Ra 9266 Overview History Legislative Intent And Key Definitions** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?
## RA 9266 Overview: History, Legislative Intent, and Key Definitions

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Explain what RA 9266 replaced and its legislative purpose.
- Describe the PRBoA composition (3 members: 1 Chair, 2 Members), their qualifications, and term limits.
- Distinguish Architect-of-Record, Architect-in-Charge of Construction, and Consulting Architect under RA 9266 §3 and IRR §3.
- Correctly cite the sections that govern definitions (§3), PRBoA creation (§4), and signing/sealing (§33).

### The Repeal and Succession of Laws

Republic Act No. 9266, the Architecture Act of 2004, was signed into law on March 17, 2004, and took effect immediately upon signature. It replaced Republic Act No. 545 of 1950, which had governed architecture practice for 54 years.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Tip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: Think of it as a generational upgrade: RA 545 (1950) served the post-war generation of architects. RA 9266 (2004) modernized regulation for the 21st century — expanding scope, strengthening board powers, and introducing continuing professional development.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

### Legislative Intent

The IRR of RA 9266 articulates the state's commitment: to develop competent, virtuous, productive, and well-rounded professional architects whose standards are excellent, qualitative, world-class, and globally competitive. The law shifts regulatory oversight from a simple licensing model to a structured governance regime with a dedicated board, comprehensive scope-of-practice definitions, and graduated disciplinary mechanisms.

---

### The PRBoA: Structure and Appointment

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="ra9266", section="Section 4"
- Text: The Professional Regulatory Board of Architecture (PRBoA) is created under Section 4 of RA 9266. It is a collegial body under the administrative supervision of the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC).
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The Board has three members: a Chairman and two Members. They are appointed by the President of the Philippines from a list of five nominees per position. The nominees come from the **Integrated and Accredited Professional Organization of Architects (IAPOA)** — now the United Architects of the Philippines (UAP) — as designated by Section 4.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: The flagging audit found a common error in earlier materials: **Section 41** does NOT designate IAPOA. Section 41 is about implementing rules and regulations. The correct reference is **Section 4**. This distinction has appeared in LEA questions.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Qualifications required:**

1. Filipino citizen and resident of the Philippines
2. BS Architecture degree from a CHED-recognized school (Philippines or abroad)
3. Valid Certificate of Registration and Professional ID Card, with at least 10 years of active architectural practice
4. Not employed as a faculty member where architecture is taught (unless fully resigned for at least 5 years before nomination)
5. No criminal conviction involving moral turpitude
6. Not a current elected officer of IAPOA/UAP or any other architects' professional organization

### Terms of Office

All three members serve **three-year terms** with staggered initial appointments. Members can be reappointed for one additional term only — maximum tenure is six years.

The staggered system ensures at least one new member joins each year during the initial cycle. This prevents one administration from appointing an entirely new Board at once.

---

### Effective Date and Organizational Timeline

> **Flag correction:** The original article stated the organizational deadline was calculated from the IRR's effective date. This is incorrect.

The law itself (RA 9266) states: *"The Board shall be organized not later than six (6) months from the effectivity of the Architecture Act of 2004"* — meaning from the law itself, not the IRR.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="ra9266", section="Section 4"
- Text: Section 4 of the IRR: "The Board shall be organized not later than six (6) months from the effectivity of the Architecture Act of 2004."
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The IRR became effective on December 1, 2004 (15 days after publication, per Section 47). RA 9266 itself was effective March 17, 2004. The six-month deadline runs from **March 17, 2004** — the law's own effectivity date.

---

### Architecture Defined

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="ra9266", section="Section 3"
- Text: RA 9266 defines architecture as *"the art, science, or profession of planning, designing, and constructing buildings in their totality taking into account their environment, in accordance with the principles of utility, strength, and beauty."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

This tripartite standard — utility, strength, beauty — echoes the Vitruvian principles embedded in architecture education globally. The law recognizes that architects operate at the intersection of aesthetic, functional, structural, and environmental considerations.

---

### Key Roles Under the Law

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:

- Text: **Architect-of-Record (AoR):** The registered and licensed architect directly and professionally responsible for the total design of the project. The AoR assumes civil liability for the plans, specifications, and contract documents signed and sealed, under Article 1723 of the Civil Code.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0010 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:

- Text: **Consulting Architect:** An academically and professionally qualified architect with exceptional expertise in a branch of architecture. The Consulting Architect assumes **no civil liability** for the project under Article 1723 unless interfering with the AoR's functions — but is liable under their own service agreements.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0011 component="Example" status="preserved"]

You bring in a Consulting Architect for specialized knowledge on healthcare design. You (the AoR) carry primary liability. The consultant is liable only under their separate agreement. If the consultant starts overriding your design decisions, they can become liable under Article 1723.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

### Structural Conceptualization

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0012 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

Section 20 is about the seal, issuance, and use of the architect's seal — not about design scope. The correct reference is **Section 3(4)(a) or Section 3(5)** of the IRR, which define the scope of practice and structural conceptualization.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

Structural conceptualization is part of the architect's scope. However, the **preparation and signing of structural design documents** remains the exclusive domain of licensed structural engineers. Architects conceptualize; engineers calculate and certify. This boundary prevents scope overlap while acknowledging the collaborative nature of building design.

---

### The Integrated and Accredited Professional Organization

The IAPOA (now UAP) is the organization from which PRBoA nominees are drawn, per **Section 4** of RA 9266. This ensures Board members remain accountable to the profession. Only registered Filipino architects with current professional standing can serve.

---

### Standard-Setting and CPD

The law tasks the PRBoA with adopting the Code of Ethical Conduct and Standards of Professional Practice. It also mandates a Continuing Professional Development (CPD) program, with CPD attendance required for renewal of the Professional Identification Card.

| Distinction | "How does an AoR differ from a Consulting Architect regarding liability?" |
| Qualification | "How many years of practice are required for PRBoA membership?" (Answer: 10 years) |

---

### Common Misunderstandings

- **Section 41 vs. Section 4:** Section 41 is about IRR adoption, NOT about IAPOA nomination. Section 4 designates IAPOA.
- **Section 20(a) vs. Section 3:** Section 20 is about the architect's seal. Structural conceptualization is defined in Section 3(5) within the Scope of Practice.
- **"Staggered terms" on the PRBoA:** All three serve 3-year terms, but initial appointments are staggered so terms expire in different years.

---

### Practice

**Recall:**
Which section of RA 9266 creates the Professional Regulatory Board of Architecture?

**Apply:**
You are an architect with 8 years of experience and a BS Architecture degree. Can you serve on the PRBoA? Why or why not?

**Transfer:**
