# SPP Document 204-A: Standards of Professional Practice on Fulltime Supervision Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 204-A: Standards of Professional Practice on Fulltime Supervision Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 204-A** governs **Fulltime Supervision Services** — the engagement of an architect or a Construction Supervision Group (CSG) to provide continuous, on-site, eight-hour-a-day construction supervision for a building project in the Philippines. It is part of the 2010 Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), promulgated as the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004), and replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 204-A**.

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the scope and compensation for SPP Doc 204-A Full-Time Supervision Services: the architect's duties during construction (daily inspection, quality control verification, interpretation of contract documents, preparation of change orders); distinguish full-time supervision from the periodic observation included in SPP 202 Phase 5; apply the monthly salary basis or percentage-of-salary compensation.
---
This document directly addresses the gap left by SPP 202 Regular Design Services, which only requires the architect to make **periodic site visits** during the construction phase — not full-time 8-hour daily supervision. When a client requires more rigorous, continuous on-site oversight, SPP 204-A provides the separate framework for that engagement.

***

## Legal and Regulatory Basis

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="authority", title="Legal Authority: R.A. No. 9266 — The Architecture Act of 2004"
- Text: This SPP document is promulgated as part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266**, approved 27 July 2010. Compliance is mandatory for all Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) and Architectural Firms (AFs) in the Philippines.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

Fulltime Supervision Services must be rendered by a **Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA)** acting as the **Architect-in-charge of construction (Aicc)**. The Aicc is **directly and professionally responsible and civilly liable** for the construction supervision of the project.

Under **Article 1723 of the New Civil Code of the Philippines**, if an engineer or architect supervises the construction, he shall be **solidarily liable** with the contractor for damages should the structure collapse or fail within 15 years from completion due to defects in the construction or materials. This is the primary legal reason why fulltime supervision carries both greater responsibility and greater professional fee than the periodic inspection role under SPP 202.

***

## Background: The Evolution of Construction Supervision

For the past 50 years, four principal members have been involved in the design and building construction process:

1. **The Owner** — who orders the implementation of the project
2. **The Architect and Specialist Consultants (SCs)** — who render plan/design services and **limited** inspection work (under SPP 202)
3. **The Contractor** — who performs the actual construction work
4. **Individuals who assist in the supervision and delivery of the work** — traditionally a Clerk-of-Works, and now the CSG (under SPP 204-A)

The evolution from the Clerk-of-Works to the CSG reflects the growing size and complexity of construction projects:

- **Clerk-of-Works era**: When projects were manageable in scale, the architect was assisted by a single construction inspector — the Clerk-of-Works — who monitored day-to-day work on behalf of the architect and owner
- **CSG era**: As projects became larger and more technically complex, a single individual was no longer adequate. The **Construction Supervision Group (CSG)** — comprising several qualified inspectors — became necessary for continuous, multi-discipline on-site inspection

***

## The Construction Supervision Group (CSG)

The **Construction Supervision Group (CSG)** is the operational core of SPP 204-A. Key facts about the CSG:

- It is **normally recommended by the Architect** based on performance track record
- It is **hired directly by the Owner** (not the architect) — the Owner pays the CSG's fees separately
- It is **answerable to both the Owner and the Architect**
- It may be constituted as a qualified architectural firm or as individual licensed professionals

This dual accountability structure — answerable to both Owner and Architect — is a critical legal and operational feature. The CSG must comply with the architect's technical directions while simultaneously reporting the project's progress and status to the owner.

***

## Scope of Services

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="lea-watch"
- Text: **SPP 204-A (Fulltime Supervision)** vs. **SPP 204-B (Construction Management)** is a classic LEA trap. 204-A means the architect is physically on-site full-time and is personally liable for construction quality. 204-B is a management/coordination role — the architect does not directly supervise tradesmen.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

SPP 204-A defines four primary service areas for fulltime supervision. Detailed tasks are specified under the Architect's Guidelines:

### 2.1 Quality Control

Quality control under SPP 204-A covers the systematic verification that all construction work meets the standards established in the Contract Documents. A **Quality Control Plan (QCP)** generally covers:

- **Project personnel** — ensuring qualifications and deployment of key construction staff
- **Quality communication** — information flow between architect, CSG, contractor, and owner
- **Quality assurance surveillance** — regular monitoring of work in progress
- **Subcontractors and suppliers** — verification of credentials, materials, and compliance
- **Project quality specifications** — benchmark standards for materials, finishes, and workmanship
- **Inspections and tests** — schedules and protocols for material testing and site inspections
- **Control of non-conformance** — processes for documenting and rectifying defective work
- **Project implementation schedule** — tracking construction milestones against approved program

### 2.2 Evaluation of Construction Work

The CSG continuously evaluates the executed work against the approved **Contract Documents** (construction drawings and technical specifications) prepared under SPP 202. Evaluation covers:

- **Conformance** of completed works to approved plans, details, and specifications
- **Workmanship quality** — whether methods and finishes meet professional and contractual standards
- **Progress** — whether construction is proceeding in accordance with the approved project implementation schedule
- **Material compliance** — whether materials used match those specified or approved alternatives

### 2.3 Preparation of Daily Inspection Reports

The CSG prepares **Daily Inspection Reports (DIR)** documenting:

- Work accomplished during the day (type of work, location, quantities)
- Labor and equipment deployed by the contractor
- Materials delivered and tested on-site
- Weather conditions
- Observations on quality and conformance
- Instructions issued to the contractor
- Any disputes, incidents, or deviations from the Contract Documents

These reports serve as the primary contemporaneous record of the construction process and are essential for resolving future disputes, preparing progress billings, and establishing the factual basis for change orders.

### 2.4 Filing of Documents

The CSG maintains an organized filing system of all project documentation, including:

- Daily Inspection Reports
- Approved and pending Change Orders
- Shop drawings and material submittals
- Test reports and inspection certificates
- Correspondence between owner, architect, CSG, and contractor
- Progress photographs
- As-built drawing mark-ups

***

## Scope of Services at a Glance

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Service | What the CSG Does | Key Output | |---|---|---| | **Quality Control** | Verifies compliance with Contract Documents through QCP | Quality Control Plan, inspection certificates | | **Evaluation of Construction Work** | Assesses conformance, workmanship, progress, and materials | Progress evaluation reports | | **Daily Inspection Reports** | Documents daily activities, observations, and instructions | Daily Inspection Reports (DIR) | | **Filing of Documents** | Organizes all project rec
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Manner of Providing Services

There are **two ways** by which the Architect may enter into contract with the Owner for Fulltime Supervision Services:

### 3.1 Dual Capacity: Architect-of-record + Consulting Architect for Fulltime Supervision (or as the CSG)

In this arrangement, the Architect serves simultaneously as the **Architect-of-record (Aor)** for the design and as the **Consulting Architect for fulltime supervision**. This is generally the preferred arrangement because:

- As the Aor, the architect is in the **best position to interpret drawings and documents** and assure conformity by the Contractor — the architect knows the design intent better than anyone
- The architect can **assign staff from his own office** (technical staff, draftsmen, or site inspectors) to undertake the fulltime supervisory work as enumerated in the Architect's Guidelines
- Communication between design intent and on-site execution is seamless, reducing the risk of misinterpretation

### 3.2 Consulting Architect Only (or as the CSG)

In this arrangement, the Architect is engaged **solely to provide fulltime supervision services**, with a different architect serving as the Aor for the project. This may occur when:

- The design architect is based in a different city or region and cannot provide on-site supervision
- The owner prefers to engage a separate specialist firm for construction supervision
- The project involves a design-builder (under SPP 207) who has a separate design team

***

## Method of Compensation

Compensation for Fulltime Supervision Services is based on the Architect's/architectural firm's **tleants, skill, experience**, and on the **type and level of professional services provided**. Six methods may be applied:

### 4.1 Percentage (%) of Project Construction Cost (PCC)

The most common basis for fulltime supervision fees. The specific percentage applicable to each project type and PCC range is detailed in the **Architect's Guidelines**. Note that the supervision fee is a **separate percentage** on top of the Regular Design Services fee under SPP 202; they are not combined into a single rate.

### 4.2 Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses (MDPE)

Applicable where the cost of professional time is the most equitable basis. The formula is:

\[
\text\{Direct Cost\} = (A \times AN) + (C \times CN) + (T \times TN)
\]

\[
\text\{Fee\} = \text\{Direct Cost\} \times M
\]

\[
\text\{Total Cost to Client\} = \text\{Fee\} + R
\]

Where:
- \(A\) = Architect's rate per hour
- \(C\) = Consultant's rate per hour
- \(T\) = Rate per hour of Technical Staff, Inspectors, and others involved in the project
- \(AN, CN, TN\) = Number of hours spent by each party
- \(M\) = Multiplier (ranging from **1.5 to 2.5**) to account for overhead and reasonable profit, depending on the office set-up and complexity of the project
- \(R\) = Reimbursable expenses (transportation, out-of-town living allowances for staff assigned more than 100 km from the office, extra printing, overseas communications, lab tests, etc.)

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: The architect must disclose to the client, **at the start of the commission**, the rates of professionals and personnel assigned to the project and the multiplier to be applied, before agreeing on this method.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

### 4.3 Professional Fee Plus Expenses

Used where there is a **continuing relationship** involving a series of projects. A fixed sum is established above and beyond reimbursement for the architect's technical time and overhead. An agreement on the general scope of work is required to set an equitable fee.

### 4.4 Lump Sum or Fixed Fee

Applied where the **scope of supervision work is well-defined** and predictable — most commonly for government projects, which entail more paperwork and time-consuming administrative processes.

### 4.5 Per Diem, Honorarium Plus Reimbursable Expenses

Applied when the architect's personal time is required for specific site visits, conferences, or project-related meetings — particularly appropriate for limited-duration assignments or when the architect is based far from the project site.

### 4.6 Mixed Methods of Compensation

More than one method may be applied to a single project. For example, the principal architect's oversight role may be compensated on a Professional Fee Plus Expenses basis, while the CSG's daily site work is compensated through MDPE.

***

### Compensation Methods at a Glance

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Method | Best Used For | Key Feature | |---|---|---| | % of PCC | All regular construction projects | Separate rate from SPP 202 design fee | | MDPE | Variable-scope, research-intensive work | Multiplier 1.5–2.5 on personnel hours | | Professional Fee + Expenses | Ongoing/repeat client relationships | Fixed sum + reimbursements | | Lump Sum / Fixed Fee | Government projects; well-defined scope | Predictable total cost | | Per Diem + Honorarium | Short or site-visit-only engagements | Daily rat
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Limitation of Authority

The CSG's authority is deliberately bounded to protect the integrity of the construction process and avoid legal entanglements:

- The CSG shall **not assume the responsibility of the Contractor's project superintendent** — that is, it must not directly manage, direct, or control the contractor's workforce or methods
- The CSG shall **not involve itself directly with the contractor's work** in any way that could be construed as assuming the contractor's liability under Article 1723 of the Civil Code
- The CSG shall **not impose methods, systems, or designs** that will substantially affect the construction schedule or impair the design concept of the Architect

These limitations exist to maintain the clear separation between the **professional role** (verification and reporting) and the **contractual role** (execution and delivery). Blurring this line exposes the CSG — and by extension the Aor — to broader legal liability.

***

## Legal Responsibility and Civil Liability

### Chain of Responsibility

Under SPP 204-A, the legal chain of responsibility is distributed as follows:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Party | Responsibility | |---|---| | **Owner** | Makes decisions on the project; ensures funds are available | | **Architect-of-record (Aor)** | Professional responsibility for design; technical oversight of the CSG | | **Engineers-of-record (Eors)** | Responsible for their respective engineering plans | | **Contractor** | Responsible for his personnel, equipment, and delivery of the project | | **CSG (Fulltime Supervisor)** | On-site quality control, evaluation, reporting, and document filing
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

### Cross-Claims and Civil Liability

If the **Aor and Eors are sued by an Owner** for civil liabilities traceable to the CSG's performance or non-performance, the Aor and Eors may **file cross-claims against the CSG**. This is a significant legal protection for the design architect: the law allows the Aor to seek indemnification from the CSG for liabilities that properly belong to the CSG's supervision failures, rather than to design deficiencies.

Conversely, if the architect supervises construction (taking on the Aicc role), Article 1723 of the Civil Code explicitly provides that the architect **shall be solidarily liable with the contractor** for structural defects that manifest within 15 years from project completion. This solidary liability is the most compelling reason why fulltime supervision carries a significantly higher fee and requires a separate, written Owner-Architect Agreement.

***

## Qualifications of CSG Inspectors

Inspectors of the Construction Supervision Group (CSG) must possess:

1. **A Bachelor of Science in Architecture (B.S. Arch.) degree** — Only licensed architects are qualified to serve as CSG inspectors under SPP 204-A
2. **Extensive experience in design and building construction** — The inspector must have sufficient practical exposure to construction methods, materials, and sequencing to properly evaluate field work
3. **Thorough knowledge of building materials and construction detailing** — The inspector must be able to read and interpret Contract Documents, identify non-conforming work, and advise the contractor on correct execution methods

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: **Note:** The SPP does not specify a minimum number of years of experience. The "extensive experience" standard is evaluated qualitatively, in consultation with the Architect and Owner. In practice, a CSG inspector is expected to have no fewer than 3–5 years of relevant field experience.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## SPP 202 Periodic Inspection vs. SPP 204-A Fulltime Supervision

A frequently misunderstood distinction is the difference between the architect's **periodic construction phase visits under SPP 202** and the **fulltime supervision engagement under SPP 204-A**:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | | SPP 202 (Periodic Site Visits) | SPP 204-A (Fulltime Supervision) | |---|---|---| | **Frequency** | Periodic, as needed | Daily, 8 hours per day | | **Personnel** | Architect-of-record or representative | CSG (full team of inspectors) | | **Primary purpose** | Familiarize with progress; issue Certificates for Payment | Continuous quality control, evaluation, and reporting | | **Daily reports** | Not required | Required (Daily Inspection Reports) | | **Liability for construction defects** | N
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Relationship to Other SPP Documents

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | SPP Document | Relationship | |---|---| | **SPP Doc. 202** (Regular Design Services) | SPP 202 Construction Phase includes only periodic visits; SPP 204-A is the formal expansion of that role into fulltime on-site supervision | | **SPP Doc. 204-B** (Construction Management) | SPP 204-B expands the CSG's role into broader project management (cost/time control, coordination); the CM's responsibilities include and subsume the CSG's SPP 204-A functions | | **SPP Doc. 206** (Comprehensive Architect
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**
- The Aicc role under SPP 204-A triggers **solidary liability** under Article 1723 of the Civil Code — do not informally assume fulltime supervision without a proper written agreement and separate fee arrangement.
- When acting in dual capacity (Aor + fulltime supervisor), maintain clear records distinguishing design-phase services from supervision-phase services, as these are separately compensated.
- The CSG works under the architect's technical direction but is hired and paid by the owner — document all instructions to the CSG in writing to establish a clear chain of technical authority.

**For Clients / Project Proponents:**
- Fulltime supervision is **not included** in the regular architect's fee under SPP 202 — budget for it as a separate line item from the outset.
- The CSG is recommended by the architect but **paid by the owner directly** — the CSG fee does not pass through the architect's accounts.
- Engaging a CSG is most advisable for large, complex, or high-value projects where construction quality, material conformance, and progress control are critical — the cost of supervision is typically far lower than the cost of construction defects discovered after turnover.
- Ensure the Owner-Architect Agreement for SPP 204-A clearly states: the scope of the CSG, the number of inspectors, their schedules, the method of compensation, and the reporting structure.

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Swipe: Full-time supervision (204-A) vs Construction Administration (SPP 202 Phase 5): FTS = DAILY on-site inspection, CA = periodic observation. Five FTS duties: (1) Daily quality control, (2) Verify conformance to plans, (3) Interpret contract documents, (4) Prepare change orders, (5) Maintain daily log. Compensation = monthly salary or percentage of salary.

Five FTS duties: (1) Daily quality control, (2) Verify conformance to plans, (3) Interpret contract documents, (4) Prepare change orders, (5) Maintain daily log. Compensation = monthly salary or percentage of salary.

## SPP Doc 202 Overview: The Six-Phase Framework and Its Design Logic
## Learning Goal
After reading this article, you should understand the key concepts tested in the LEA for this topic, including relevant code provisions, dimensional standards, and common exam applications.

SPP Document 202 defines regular design services under a six-phase framework that organizes the architect's work from project definition through construction administration. The document addresses both individual and group architectural practice while clarifying foreign architect requirements and business process outsourcing restrictions for Philippine projects.

### The Six Phases of Regular Design Services

### Fee Distribution Across Phases

The five fee-earning phases under SPP 202 are distributed as follows: Schematic Design earns 15% of the Project Construction Cost fee, Design Development earns 20%, Contract Documents earns 50%, Bidding Assistance earns 5%, and Construction Administration earns 10%. ## Phases 4 and 5: Bidding Assistance and Construction Administration Under SPP 202
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

- Describe the Bidding or Negotiation Phase activities: bid document preparation, pre-bid conference, bid analysis, and award recommendation.
- Describe the Construction Administration Phase activities: site visits, payment certification, change order review, and project closeout.
- Distinguish the Architect's role in bidding assistance from the construction administration role.
- Apply Phases 5 and 6 requirements to LEA scenarios involving bid evaluation, contract award, and construction-phase services.

SPP 202 identifies six phases of regular design services: Project Definition Phase, Schematic Design Phase, Design Development Phase, Contract Documents Phase, Bidding or Negotiation Phase, and Construction Phase. Bidding Assistance and Construction Administration are the fifth and sixth phases.—complete the architect's engagement with the project. According to SPP 202, the Contract Documents Phase represents 90% of the architect's total design fees. The specific percentage allocations for Bidding Assistance and Construction Administration phases are not explicitly detailed in SPP 202 as separate percentages.

### Bidding Assistance Phase Activities

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="ArticleMedia" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: id="media-lea-prac-svc-008-phases-4-and-5-bidding-", type="image", caption="Phases 4 & 5 — Bidding Assistance and Construction Administration Workflow", description="Workflow chart showing the Bidding Assistance Phase activities (bid document preparation, pre-bid conference, bid analysis, award recommendation) transitioning into the Construction Administration Phase (site visits, payment certification, change order review, project closeout).", suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image", status="placeholder"
- Text: (none detected)
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

In the Bidding or Negotiation Phase, the architect prepares bid documents including forms for contract letting, construction documents, invitation and instruction to bidders, forms for bidders' proposals, and general or specific conditions of contract. The architect assists the owner from the early stage of establishing a list of prospective contractors. For competitive bids, the architect furnishes complete sets of Bid Documents loaned to bidders covering direct and indirect costs. The architect helps organize and conduct pre-bid conferences, responds to bidder questions, and assists in obtaining proposals and analyzing bid results.

### Construction Administration Phase

Construction Administration begins after the contractor commences work and continues until final project completion and turnover to the owner. The architect makes decisions on all owner and contractor claims relating to execution and progress of work or interpretation of Contract Documents. The architect issues certificates for payment based on observed contractor work quality and contractual compliance. The architect makes periodic site visits to familiarize himself with construction progress and ensure work proceeds according to Contract Documents, though full-time supervision is available as a separately compensated service.

### Fee Distribution and Timeline

Bidding Assistance earns 5% of total fees, representing the shortest phase. Construction Administration earns 10%, the second-smallest percentage despite its extended timeline. According to SPP 202, the Contract Documents Phase represents 90% of total design services fees. The remaining phases (Project Definition, Schematic Design, Design Development, Bidding Assistance, and Construction Administration) collectively represent the remaining 10%. This modest allocation reflects that by construction, the major design work is complete, even though significant coordination and oversight activities continue. The architect's role shifts from creator to administrator and inspector of the design.

# SPP Document 203: Standards of Professional Practice on Specialized Architectural Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 203: Standards of Professional Practice on Specialized Architectural Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 203** governs **Specialized Architectural Services** — a broad and evolving category of architectural practice covering expertise needed to complete, complement, or supplement the totality of any building or planning project. It is part of the 2010 Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), promulgated as the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004), and replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 203**.

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the nine categories of specialized architectural services under SPP Doc 203 — interior design, landscape architecture, acoustical design, lighting design, preservation/conservation, space planning, urban design, graphic design, and expert witness services — and explain how each is scoped, compensated (per-diem, fixed fee, or percentage), and documented separately from basic services.
---
SPP 203 recognizes that architecture, as the blending of aesthetics, functions, space, materials and environment, now requires the application of various technologies and specialized skills that go beyond what is covered in SPP 202 Regular Design Services. It contains **23 enumerated sub-specialties** (203.1 through 203.23), each constituting a distinct area of advanced or specialized architectural practice.

***

## Legal and Regulatory Basis

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="authority", title="Legal Authority: R.A. No. 9266 — The Architecture Act of 2004"
- Text: This SPP document is promulgated as part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266**, approved 27 July 2010. Compliance is mandatory for all Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) and Architectural Firms (AFs) in the Philippines.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

All specialized architectural services under SPP 203 must be rendered by a **Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA)** acting as a **Consulting Architect (CA)**. The Consulting Architect may also be a separately Registered and Licensed Professional (RLP) — meaning the CA may hold a valid professional identification card for one or more State-regulated professions other than architecture (e.g., Environmental Planner, Landscape Architect). The Board and the Commission may issue a **Specialist Certificate** to a qualifying RLA, upon accreditation by the IAPOA.

The architect's responsibility under SPP 203 remains consistent: to ensure that both the building and its physical environment enhance the lives of people by strictly adhering to national and international standards with regard to **public health, safety, and welfare**.

***

## General Structure of Each Sub-Service

For each of the 23 specialized services, SPP 203 follows a consistent structure:

1. **Introduction** — Context and rationale for the service
2. **Scope of Services** — Specific tasks the Consulting Architect performs
3. **Manner of Providing Services** — How the Architect may be engaged (dual capacity or consulting only)
4. **Method of Compensation** — How fees are determined

For the first six sub-services (203.1–203.6), which involve extensive work, the SPP provides full introductions and detailed scopes. For sub-services 203.7–203.23, the SPP provides focused descriptions without full four-part breakdowns, deferring to the **Architect's Guidelines** for fee structures and detailed procedures.

### Manner of Providing Services (Common to All Sub-Services)

For all specialized services, the architect may enter into contract with the owner in two ways:

1. **Dual capacity** — acting simultaneously as Architect-of-record (Aor) and as Consulting Architect for the specialized service
2. **Consulting Architect only** — engaged solely to provide the specialized service, with another architect serving as Aor

***

## The 23 Specialized Architectural Services

### Group A: Design and Aesthetic Services

#### 203.1 Architectural Interior (AI) Services

**Introduction:** Architectural Interiors (AI), specifically mentioned under Secs. 3(4)(g) and 14(3) of R.A. No. 9266, involves the detailed planning and design of the indoor/enclosed areas of any proposed building or structure, including retrofit, renovation, rehabilitation, or expansion work covering all architectural and utility aspects, including the architectural lay-outing of all building engineering systems.

**Scope of Services:** The Consulting Architect for AI:
- Prescribes space plans, stacking diagrams/sections, and computations of areas for the different activities and spaces
- Lays out and prescribes furniture, built-ins, and equipment; prepares specifications of AI components including all floor/wall/ceiling finishes, doors and partition systems, hardware, modular or ready-assembled furniture, built-ins, fixtures, signages, and graphic devices
- Assists the client in conducting bids or negotiations with general contractors, sub-contractors, and suppliers
- Checks and approves samples of materials and shop drawings of AI components
- Reviews and approves billings of AI components
- Conducts final inspection and approves installed AI components

**Method of Compensation:** For projects involving extensive detailing of AI components such as custom floor, wall, ceiling construction and finishes, cabinet design, built-in components, equipment, and special fittings, the fee is a **percentage of the cost of the AI work**. Should the client separately hire Specialist Consultants, their fee is for the account of the client directly.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: **Note:** AI under SPP 203 refers specifically to the architectural aspect of interiors — space planning, utility lay-outing, built-ins, and specifications — as distinct from the separate and separately licensed profession of **Interior Design**.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

#### 203.2 Acoustic Design Services

**Introduction:** Acoustic Design Services involve the detailed planning and design to control sound transmission for compatibility with the architectural design concept. The evolution of products and techniques in sound management has provided greater flexibility in designing interior environments that respond to acoustical demands of varied activities.

**Scope of Services:** The Consulting Architect for Acoustic Design:
- Prepares drawings and specifications for acoustic design and treatment, sound control and reinforcement, sound absorption, reflectance, and insulation
- Assists the owner/client in bidding out the work or negotiating with a specialty sub-contractor
- Checks and approves samples of materials and equipment
- Conducts final inspection of work and equipment
- Assists the owner/client in evaluating the amount due the sub-contractor

**Method of Compensation:** Fee depends on the **complexity of the works to be undertaken**. Any separately hired Specialist Consultants are paid directly by the client.

***

#### 203.3 Architectural Lighting Layout and Design

**Introduction:** Architectural Lighting Layout and Design involves the detailed planning and design of light transmission, timing, and control for compatibility with the architectural design concept. It addresses the lighting demands of varied activities within and outside a building.

**Scope of Services:** The Consulting Architect for Lighting Design:
- Prepares drawings and specifications for lighting design, illumination, fixture placement, efficiency, and energy considerations
- Assists the owner/client in bidding out the work or negotiating with specialty sub-contractors
- Checks and approves samples of materials and fixtures
- Conducts final inspection of work and fixtures
- Assists owner/client in evaluating the amount due the sub-contractor

**Method of Compensation:** Fee depends on the **complexity of the works to be undertaken**. "Cost of the Work" means the total cost of all fixtures and accessories designed, specified, or procured by the Specialist Architect and/or Specialist Consultants for the owner/client that were used or installed in the project.

***

### Group B: Planning and Urban Design Services

#### 203.4 Site Development Planning (SDP) Services

**Introduction:** The space planning, architectural lay-outing, and utilization of spaces within and surrounding a building must be a well-coordinated effort so that both the building and its host environment act as one. The Architect is not merely concerned with the building itself, but with the grounds and surrounding space as well.

**Scope of Services:** The Consulting Architect for SDP:
- Conceptualizes the entire Site Development Plan (SDP), including the generic scope of civil works and the general scope of softscape (plants, grass, trees) and hardscape (paving, walls, water features) requirements
- Conceptualizes the specifications for the needed civil works and utility lines
- Assists the owner/client in bidding out work or negotiating with landscape, waterscape, and rock formation contractors

**Method of Compensation:** Fee depends on the **estimated cost of civil works and landscaping works** (hardscape and softscape), depending on magnitude and complexity. If the architect is also certified and licensed as a Landscape Architect (RLP), the fee increases correspondingly. If the owner separately engages a Landscape Architect, that fee is for the owner's direct account.

***

#### 203.5 Site and Physical Planning Services (Including Master Development Planning, Subdivision Planning, and Urban Design)

**Introduction:** Physical planning refers to the orderly arrangement within a piece of land or property on which vertical structures and horizontal developments (ROWs, open spaces, activity spaces) are to be proposed. The great cities of the world took shape through the activities of visionary architects who actively engaged in physical planning.

**Scope of Services:** The Consulting Architect for Site and Physical Planning:
- Confers with the owner/client, secures primary and secondary data for reliable projections and analyses
- Examines laws, ordinances, rules, and regulations (code searches) and considers best industry practices
- Prepares Framework and Conceptual Master Development Plans (FRDPs and CMDPs) and reports
- Prepares Preliminary up to Detailed Master Development Plans (PMDPs/DMDPs) showing: physical layout, road networks, vehicular and pedestrian movement, legal easements, basic utility layouts, landscape layouts, lot pad elevations, lot primacy matrices, deed of restrictions (DoR), development standards and guidelines (DSG), lot counts, land use tabulations, building footprints, roof-prints, view corridors, and building cast shadow projections
- Prepares the SPPCC for the total physical development
- Undertakes modifications and revisions as required within the engagement period
- Prepares finalized plans, reports, and specifications for government approval
- Prepares phasing of construction with the concurrence of the owner

**Typical Sites:** Industrial estates, commercial centers, religious/institutional/government/civic centers, sports complexes, tourism estates/resorts, amusement parks, educational facilities, residential/housing subdivisions.

**Method of Compensation:** Fee structure as stated in the **Architect's Guidelines**.

***

#### 203.6 Comprehensive Development Planning (CDP) Services

**Introduction:** CDP is an expanded form of physical planning that includes all activities necessary for formulating, implementing, and realizing a Master Development Plan (MDP), including the preparation of Environmental Impact Assessments/Statements (EIA/S). While the MDP puts premium on physical planning and engineering, CDP emphasizes non-physical components — financial, economic/market, socio-cultural, administrative-political-institutional-legal, and environmental.

**Scope of Services (Five CDP Components)**:
1. **Physical Component** — Land use and changes in the physical environment, represented by the MDP
2. **Economic Component** — The nation's assets and their management
3. **Socio-Cultural Component** — People, their living conditions, and ways to ameliorate them
4. **Transport Component** — Road and transit networks, land-sea-air linkages, movement of people and goods
5. **Legal and Administrative Component** — The relationship of development proposals and policies to existing laws

The Consulting Architect performing CDP:
- Identifies existing land use, resources, social behavior, and interaction
- Undertakes environmental analysis, demographic analysis, and feasibility studies
- Examines existing laws, ordinances, and political/social constraints
- Prepares conceptual development plans, policies, and implementing strategies to arrive at CDP solutions

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: **Note:** CDP ideally requires the architect to also be a separately qualified and licensed **Environmental Planner (EnP)**. If not, the Architect must engage duly qualified professionals as Specialist Consultants.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


**Method of Compensation:** Through **man-months** (22 man-days × 8 man-hours/day), multiplied by a factor covering overhead and other direct/indirect costs, as prescribed in the Architect's Guidelines.

***

### Group C: Heritage and Safety Services

#### 203.7 Historic and Cultural Heritage Conservation and Planning

The Consulting Architect in this specialized area provides **research, assessment, recording, management, interpretation, and conservation of historical heritage**. This requires deep knowledge of history, materials, and conservation protocols such as the Venice Charter and applicable Philippine heritage laws (e.g., R.A. No. 10066, the National Cultural Heritage Act).

***

#### 203.8 Security Evaluation and Planning

The Consulting Architect in this area **arranges and formulates methods of rating and ascertaining the value of structures or facilities** which must be fully secured, kept safe, protected, and provided with sufficient safeguards for the conduct of any work or activity. This includes security system design, threat/risk assessment, and the preparation of the **Fire Safety and Life Assessment Report (FALAR)** required by R.A. No. 9514, the 2008 Fire Code of the Philippines and its 2009 IRR.

***

### Group D: Technical and Building Systems Services

#### 203.9 Building Systems Design

The Consulting Architect in this area engages in methods of **producing building components in a highly engineered, efficient, and cost-effective manner**, particularly for residential and commercial applications. This covers the integration of structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing/sanitary, communications, and electronic systems in a manner that supports and does not conflict with the architectural design concept.

***

#### 203.10 Facilities Maintenance Support

The Consulting Architect provides the owner/client with means and measures to **ensure the proper function and maintenance of the building/structure and site after final inspection**. This includes creating maintenance programs, schedules, and guidelines for the long-term care of the building.

***

#### 203.11 Building Testing and Commissioning

The Consulting Architect **recommends the systematic process of ensuring that a building's array of systems is planned, designed, installed, and tested to perform according to design intent and operational needs**. The SPP explicitly states: if building materials, equipment, and systems are not installed properly or are not operating as intended, the effectiveness, efficiency, productivity, and other benefits of high-performance plans/designs will not be achieved.

***

#### 203.12 Building Environmental Certification

This sub-service involves the use of a **building environment rating system** to evaluate the environmental performance of a building and to encourage market migration towards sustainable design. The rating system must be:
- **Credit-based** — projects earn points for environment-friendly actions during planning, design, construction, and occupancy
- **Flexible** — projects need not meet identical requirements to qualify
- **Consensus-based and market-driven** — to accelerate the development of green building practices

The Consulting Architect must have expertise in Green Architecture, Environmental/Sustainable Design, and Philippine environmental laws (Solid Waste, Clean Air, and Clean Water Acts) and DENR administrative issuances.

***

#### 203.13 Forensic Architecture

The Consulting Architect **undertakes a scientific study on the built environment's well-being**, focusing on how a building can best maintain itself and prolong its life in a cost-efficient manner. The forensic study may include:
- Determination of causes of building, component, and/or material deterioration
- Causes of observed building deficiencies (e.g., non-compliance with planning/building laws, deviations from original use)
- Research on possible faulty activities and operations during project implementation
- Determination of faulty plan/design and/or construction methodology

***

#### 203.14 Building Appraisal

Appraisal is defined as an **act or process of estimating value**. The Consulting Architect places value on the building/structure's condition and defects, and on its repair and maintenance, including the required improvements.

***

#### 203.15 Structural Conceptualization

The Consulting Architect **conceives, chooses, and develops the type, disposition, arrangement, and proportioning of the structural elements** of an architectural work, giving due consideration to safety, cost-effectiveness, functionality, and aesthetics. Note that structural conceptualization remains within the architect's domain; detailed structural analysis and computation remain with the licensed structural engineer.

***

### Group E: Documentation and Process Services

#### 203.16 Preliminary Services

The Consulting Architect in this area must have advanced knowledge of **Site Analysis, Space Planning and Management, Architectural Programming**, and the other services under SPP Document 201. This service covers early-stage advisory and site preparation work that precedes formal design.

***

#### 203.17 Contract Documentation and Review Services

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of **Specification Writing, Estimation and Quantity Survey, Architectural Production, Architectural Software, Architectural Support Services, and Contract Document Review**. This service is particularly valuable for peer review of documents prepared by other architects or firms.

***

#### 203.18 Post-Design Services (Including Construction Services)

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of **Pre-Construction, Construction, Post-Construction**, and the other services under SPP Documents 204, 206, and 207. Included under this specialized practice is the preparation of the **Fire Safety and Life Assessment Report (FALAR)** required by R.A. No. 9514, the 2008 Fire Code of the Philippines and its 2009 IRR.

***

#### 203.19 Dispute Avoidance and Resolution

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of the various modes of **Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)** prescribed under R.A. No. 9285 (the ADR Act of 2004) and its IRR, including:
- Construction Arbitration
- Mediation and Conciliation
- Negotiation
- Contract Administration, Quality Surveys, Appraisals and Adjustments
- Expert Testimony

An architect specializing in ADR must preferably be **State-accredited**.

***

### Group F: Research, Planning, and Management Services

#### 203.20 Architectural Research Methods

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of **Research Methods, Philippine Architecture and its History, Architectural Materials and Finishes, Building Types and Standards, Architectural Design Trends, Architectural Writing, and Architectural Photography**.

***

#### 203.21 Special Building/Facility Planning and Design

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of the planning and design processes required for:
- Housing Developments
- Recreational and Tourism Estates
- Health Care and Hospitality Facilities
- Transportation and Telecommunications Facilities
- Production and Extractive Facilities
- Utility-related Developments
- Secure Facilities
- Business and Industrial Parks
- Economic Zones
- Community Architecture

***

#### 203.22 Building Components

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of **Building Materials and Finishes, Construction Methodologies, Building Envelopes** (including cladding and roofing systems), **Architectural Fenestrations**, and **Architectural Hardware, Fixtures, and Fittings**.

***

#### 203.23 Management of Architectural Practices

The Consulting Architect must have advanced knowledge of:
- Types of Architectural Office Operations and Office Management
- Accounting, Finance, Taxation, and Audit
- Labor Code
- Architectural Marketing and Project Development
- Proposals, Negotiations, and Contracts
- Contract Administration
- File Management
- Limitations of Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO) Operations

***

## Quick Reference: All 23 Specialized Services

- Text: | No. | Sub-Service | Category | Compensation Basis | |---|---|---|---| | 203.1 | Architectural Interior (AI) Services | Design & Aesthetic | % of cost of AI work | | 203.2 | Acoustic Design Services | Design & Aesthetic | Based on complexity | | 203.3 | Architectural Lighting Layout and Design | Design & Aesthetic | Based on complexity / cost of fixtures | | 203.4 | Site Development Planning (SDP) | Planning | Based on estimated cost of civil/landscaping works | | 203.5 | Site and Physical Plan
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## General Method of Compensation for All Specialized Services

All 23 specialized services may be classified as **additional or extra services** to the regular design services of SPP 202. The general compensation framework for specialized services is:

\[
\text\{Fee\} = \text\{Man-months\} \times \text\{Factor\}
\]

Where:
- **Man-month** = 22 man-days × 8 man-hours/man-day = 176 man-hours per man-month
- **Factor** = a multiplier to cover other direct and indirect costs (e.g., overhead, profit)

Any other applicable mode of fee determination from **SPP Document 201** (MDPE), **SPP Document 202** (percentage of PCC), or the **Architect's Guidelines** may also be applied, depending on the nature of the specialized service.

***

## Relationship to Other SPP Documents

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | SPP Document | Relationship to SPP 203 | |---|---| | **SPP Doc. 201** (Pre-Design) | SPP 203 services like Architectural Programming and Site Analysis are advanced extensions of pre-design tasks | | **SPP Doc. 202** (Regular Design) | SPP 203 services supplement and enhance the design delivered under SPP 202; the regular architectural plan falls under 202, while specialized components fall under 203 | | **SPP Doc. 204-A/B** (Construction) | SPP 203.18 (Post-Design Services) extends into constr
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**
- The list of 23 sub-services is explicitly stated as **"include but are not limited to"** — meaning new specialized services may be recognized by the Board and IAPOA as the profession evolves.
- Specialist Certificates may be issued by the PRBoA/PRC upon accreditation by the IAPOA. Pursuing these credentials formalizes competence in specific sub-specialties.
- When acting in a **dual capacity** (Aor + Consulting Architect for the specialized service), the architect must ensure clear delineation of responsibilities and fees in the Owner-Architect Agreement, so there is no confusion between SPP 202 and SPP 203 services and their respective fees.

**For Clients / Project Proponents:**
- SPP 203 services are **always separately contracted and compensated** from SPP 202 Regular Design Services — they are never included in the regular architect's fee unless explicitly agreed upon in writing.
- Clients who wish to engage Specialist Consultants (SCs) directly — bypassing the architect — may do so; in that case, the SC fees are paid directly by the owner and do not pass through the architect. However, a **coordination fee** is still due to the architect for managing the interface between the SC's inputs and the architectural design concept.
- For sub-services 203.5 (Physical Planning) and 203.6 (CDP) involving multi-disciplinary teams, the owner must budget separately for each Specialist Consultant's fee, as these are not covered by the architect's SPP 203 fee.

---



---

## Exam Tip

LEA Trap: Nine specialized services: Interior Design, Landscape Architecture, Acoustics, Lighting, Preservation, Space Planning, Urban Design, Graphic Design, Expert Witness. Compensation: per-diem, fixed fee, or lump sum — NOT percentage of construction cost (unless the basic services contract also uses percentage). Expert witness is the only one with a forensic/legal character.

## Cross‑References

**Spp Doc 202 Regular Design Services**, **Spp Doc 204 A Fulltime Supervision Services**, **Spp Doc 205 Post Construction Services**, **Spp Doc 209 Architectural Consulting Services Pacs**
