# SPP Document 208: Standards of Professional Practice on Architectural Design Competition (ADC)


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 208: Standards of Professional Practice on Architectural Design Competition (ADC)** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 208** governs the **Architectural Design Competition (ADC)** — the formal, regulated process by which an Owner seeks design excellence by inviting Architects to submit design proposals, judged by an independent Jury under the oversight of the IAPOA. It replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 209** and forms part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004).

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the types of architectural design competitions under SPP Doc 208 (open, invited, limited, student), the rules for jury composition and judging criteria, the architect's right to retain authorship, and the compensation requirements for competition winners and participants; distinguish a competition from a design-build procurement under RA 9184.
---
SPP 208 is structurally distinct from all other SPP documents: it does not govern a bilateral relationship between Architect and Owner, but rather a **multi-party competitive process** involving Owners, Competitors, a Professional Advisor, a Jury, Technical Advisors, and the IAPOA ADC Committee. Its provisions are drawn up in the interest of **both Project Proponents/Owners and Competitors** — ensuring fairness, design integrity, anonymity, and intellectual property protection throughout the competition process.

***

## 1. Introduction and Purpose

The purpose of SPP 208 is to state the **principles upon which competitions are based** and by which **Promoters/Owners should be guided** in organizing ADCs. A properly conducted ADC serves two strategic goals:

1. **For Owners**: Obtaining **excellence in design** for a project or development concept by accessing the widest possible range of design tleant and creative ideas
2. **For Competitors**: Providing a transparent, fair, and intellectually protected forum in which registered architects can demonstrate their design capability and compete for commissions and prize money

The ADC is one of three methods of selecting an Architect recognized under the SPP/Annex "A" framework, alongside Direct Selection and Comparative Selection.

***

## 2. Definitions and Key Parties

SPP 208 defines five principal parties and three key instruments that structure every ADC:

### 2.1 The Five Principal Parties

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Party | Definition and Role | |---|---| | **Owner** | The person or organization that undertakes or promotes an ADC with the primary objective of obtaining excellence in design for a project or development concept; issues the invitation to Architects and **finances the ADC** | | **Jury** | The people appointed by the Owner to **assess the entries**; composed of Jurors (majority are Registered Licensed Architects/RLAs), assisted by a lay Juror who represents and voices the intention of the Owne
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### 2.2 The Three Key Instruments

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Instrument | Definition | |---|---| | **Conditions** | The full competition package: program, instructions on submission, site plans, entry forms, official envelopes and labels; **drawn up by the Professional Advisor** | | **SPP on ADC** | The Philippine Standard of Professional Practice on Architectural Design Competitions — the governing document itself (SPP 208) | | **IAPOA ADC Committee** | Appointed by the IAPOA National President to **oversee all ADCs** referred to the IAPOA; the oversig
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## 3. Classification of ADCs

SPP 208 provides a multi-dimensional classification system for ADCs — by **purpose**, by **stage**, and by **openness**:

### 3.1 Classification by Purpose

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Type | Description | |---|---| | **Project ADC** | For **actual projects proposed for implementation**; the winning design will be built; first prize winner is entitled to the commission | | **Ideas Competition** | A **design and planning exercise to elucidate a problem**; not necessarily for an immediate project; aims to explore design possibilities or generate innovative concepts |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### 3.2 Classification by Stage (for Project ADCs)

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Stage Type | Description | |---|---| | **Single-Stage** | All Competitors submit complete design proposals in one submission; Jury selects winners from the full field | | **Two-Stage** | First stage narrows the field to shortlisted Competitors; selected Competitors then develop more detailed proposals for the Second Stage; **honoraria must be paid** to all Second Stage participants |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *Important rule*: A competition that has received IAPOA approval as a single-stage competition **may NOT proceed to a second stage** except with **IAPOA approval** of the Conditions and arrangements for payment of honoraria to the Competitors involved, over and above the prize money originally provided.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### 3.3 Classification by Openness (for Project ADCs)

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Openness Type | Description | |---|---| | **Open** | Any qualified registered architect may participate; maximizes the range of design entries | | **Limited by Invitation** | Only Architects specifically invited by the Owner may participate; used when the Owner prefers a pre-selected pool of known practitioners |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### 3.4 Classification by Complexity

Project ADCs are **further classified according to degree of complexity** based on the project classification system under **SPP Document 202** (Groups 1–10). This determines the required scale of the design submissions, the complexity of the program of requirements, and the appropriate prize money levels.

***

## 4. IAPOA Approval

Every ADC must pass through a mandatory IAPOA approval process **before any official announcement is made**:

### 4.1 Pre-Announcement Approval

Before the Owner makes any official announcement, **the IAPOA through the ADC Committee shall send the Owner a written approval** of:

- The draft Conditions
- The timetable
- The ADC registration fee (when required)
- The composition of the Jury

### 4.2 Public Announcement

Notice of a National ADC shall be issued by the Owner and/or the IAPOA ADC Committee Secretariat with a request for publication in **technical journals or through other media**. The announcement must:

- Be simultaneous in all media to enable all interested parties to apply
- State where and how the ADC documents may be obtained
- Confirm that the **ADC conditions have received the requisite IAPOA approval**

***

## 5. Drawing Up the ADC Conditions

The Conditions are the governing document of each individual ADC — drawn up by the Professional Advisor and approved by the IAPOA. Six key principles govern the preparation of the Conditions:

### 5.1 Anonymity — The Cardinal Rule

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"It is essential that the ANONYMITY of competitors should be maintained until the final judgment of the competition. In the interest of the competition system, rigorous measures should be taken to ensure that all parties involved adhere to this principle."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


Anonymity is the bedrock protection that ensures Jury decisions are based on **design merit alone**, free from favoritism, personal relationships, or institutional bias.

### 5.2 Equality of Conditions

The ADC conditions, including the **program of requirements of a National ADC, shall be identical for all Competitors** — no competitor shall receive information or instructions that others do not receive.

### 5.3 Mandatory Content of Conditions

The Conditions for a National ADC — whether single or two-stage, open or limited — **shall state clearly**:

- The **purpose of the ADC** and the intentions of the Owner
- The **nature of the problem** to be solved
- All the **requirements which Competitors must meet**
- A clear distinction between **mandatory requirements** (non-negotiable) and those which **permit the competitor freedom of interpretation**

### 5.4 Precision of Information

All information supplied to Competitors — social, economic, technical, geographical, and topographical — **must be specific and not open to misinterpretation**. Vague or ambiguous site information can lead to Jury disputes and grounds for disqualification challenges.

### 5.5 Submission Requirements

The Conditions must state the **number, nature, scale, and dimensions** of the documents, plans, or models required, and the terms of acceptance. Where a cost estimate is required, the Conditions must prescribe a **standard form of presentation** to ensure comparability across entries.

### 5.6 Supplementary Instructions

In a two-stage competition, **supplementary information and instructions approved by the Jury** may be issued by the Owner to all Competitors selected to proceed to the Second Stage.

***

## 6. The Professional Advisor

The Professional Advisor is the **Architect who runs the competition** on behalf of the Owner — the operational manager of the entire ADC process.

### 6.1 Appointment

Appointed and **paid by the Owner**, but must be **approved by the IAPOA National Board of Directors (NBD)** through its ADC Committee.

### 6.2 Functions

The Professional Advisor:

- Supervises the **conduct of the ADC** and prepares the **Conditions**
- Ensures the **ADC timetable** is adhered to
- Supervises the **receipt of Competitors' questions** and the **dispatch of replies to all Competitors** (ensuring all receive the same information)
- Supervises the **receipt of competition entries**
- **Safeguards the anonymity** of Competitors at all times
- **Assists the Jury** and is present during its deliberations
- Has **no vote** in Jury deliberations
- Responsibilities are **limited to the organization and conduct** of the competition only

***

## 7. The Jury

The Jury is the **decision-making body** of the ADC — its awards are final.

### 7.1 Composition Rules

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Rule | Provision | |---|---| | **Size** | Smallest reasonable number; must be an **odd number**, not to exceed **seven (7)** | | **Architect majority** | At least **4 out of 7** (majority) must be **Registered Licensed Architects (RLAs)** | | **IAPOA representative** | At least **one Architect-Juror must represent the IAPOA** | | **Owner representation** | **Not more than one (1)** representative of the Owner may be included | | **Appointment** | Jurors are **appointed by the Owner and approve
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### 7.2 Conduct Rules

- **All Jurors must be present** at all meetings of the Jury — no proxy voting
- Each Juror must **see the Conditions before** they are made available to Competitors
- Decisions are taken by **majority vote**, with a **separate vote on each competition plan/design** submitted
- Any drawings, photographs, models, or documents **not required under the regulations shall be excluded** before the Jury examines a Competitor's entry
- The Jury **shall disqualify** any design that does not conform to the mandatory requirements, instructions, or Conditions

### 7.3 Awards and Reporting

- The Jury **must make awards** — it cannot decline to award prizes
- Awards shall be **final** and made public by a date agreed on with the IAPOA and stated in the Conditions
- The Jury must make **full use of the amount set aside for prizes** in the ADC Conditions
- The **list of ADC awards and the Jury's report** shall be **signed by all Jurors** before the Jury is dissolved; one copy shall be sent to the IAPOA

### 7.4 Two-Stage Competition Rule

In a two-stage competition, **the same Jury** must judge both stages. If the competition converts from single-stage to two-stage, the **same Jury must be reappointed** by the Owner.

### 7.5 Fees

**All Jury fees, travel, and subsistence expenses shall be paid by the Owner**.

***

## 8. Persons Not Eligible for Entry

SPP 208 maintains strict conflict-of-interest exclusions to protect competition integrity:

- **No Jury member** may take part in the competition — either directly or indirectly — nor be commissioned with work connected with the prize-winning design (directly or indirectly)
- **No member of the promoting body** (Owner's organization), nor any associate or employee, nor any **person concerned with the preparation or organization of the ADC** is eligible to compete or to assist a Competitor

These exclusions apply to the **Professional Advisor** and **Competition Secretariat** members as well — anyone who had access to the Conditions before they were made available to all Competitors is barred from competing.

***

## 9. Prizes, Honoraria, and Mentions

### 9.1 General Prize Principles

- The Conditions must state the **amount and number of prizes**
- Prizes must be **related to the size and complexity of the project**, the amount of work involved, and the **expense incurred by Competitors**
- The Owner must allot **adequate prize money** to compensate all Competitors for their work
- For **Ideas Competitions only**, it may be possible to remunerate only the first-prize winner
- The Owner must pay prizes within **one (1) month** of the official announcement of ADC results

### 9.2 Honoraria Rules

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Situation | Honorarium Rule | |---|---| | **Limited ADC by Invitation** | Each participant shall receive an **honorarium in addition to the prizes** awarded | | **Two-Stage Competition (2nd Stage)** | A **reasonable honorarium shall be paid to each Competitor** selected to take part in the Second Stage — to reimburse additional work; stated in Conditions; in addition to prizes |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### 9.3 The First Prize–Commission Rule

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0010 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"In Project ADCs, the award of first prize to a plan/design places the Owner under an obligation to entrust the Author of the plan/design with the commission for the Project."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


This is the most commercially significant rule in SPP 208: winning a Project ADC **automatically entitles the winner to the full design commission** under SPP 202. The Owner cannot take the winning design and hire a different architect to implement it.

**Exception**: If the winning Competitor is **unable to satisfy the Jury of his ability to carry out the design work**, the Jury may require the winner to **collaborate with another Architect of the winning Competitor's choice**, duly approved by the Jury and Owner.

### 9.4 The 12-Month Commission Rule

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0011 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"In Project ADCs, provisions shall be made in the ADC Conditions for the first prize winner to receive compensation of a further sum equal to the amount of the first prize if no contract is signed within twelve (12) months of the announcement of the Jury's award."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


If the Owner fails to commission the winning Architect within 12 months, the winning Architect is entitled to **double the first prize amount**. Importantly: even after this additional compensation, **the Owner still does not acquire the right to carry out the project except with the collaboration of the Author**.

***

## 10. Copyright and Right of Ownership

SPP 208 establishes a **strong, unwaivable copyright framework** for all competition entries:

### 10.1 Competitor's Copyright Retained

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0012 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"The Author of any plan/design shall retain the copyright of his work; no alterations may be made without his/her written consent."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


This applies to **all entries** — winners and non-winners alike. The submission of an entry to an ADC does not transfer copyright to the Owner.

### 10.2 Winner's Design: One Execution Only

The design awarded first prize **can only be used by the Owner** upon his commissioning the Author to carry out the plan/design preparation for the project. The Owner's right to use the ADC-generated plan/design **covers one (1) execution only** — the design cannot be replicated or adapted for another project without the Author's consent.

### 10.3 No Piecemeal Use of Other Entries

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0013 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"No other plan/design may be used wholly or in part by the Owner except by agreement with the Author concerned."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


The Owner **cannot pick out portions of non-winning entries** and combine them into another design — this is explicitly prohibited. This provision is reinforced by:

- **Section 20(4) and 33 of R.A. No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004)
- **R.A. No. 8293** (Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines) and their respective IRRs

### 10.4 Ideas Competition Copyright

If the Owner in an Ideas Competition decides to make use of all or part of the winning scheme, **the collaboration of the Author is required**, and the terms must be acceptable to the Author.

***

## 11. Registration of Competitors

### 11.1 Registration Requirement and Acceptance

All Competitors must **register with the Owner** upon receiving ADC details. **Registration implies acceptance of the Conditions** of the ADC — it is a binding agreement to abide by the competition rules.

### 11.2 Documentation

The Owner shall issue to all registered Competitors **all necessary documentation** for preparing their plans/designs. If furnishing documentation is conditional on a deposit, **the deposit shall be returned** to Competitors who submit a bona fide plan/design, unless otherwise stated.

### 11.3 Two-Stage Anonymity

The names of Competitors selected to proceed to the Second Stage **shall be made public only under exceptional conditions** agreed on by the Jury before the launching of the ADC — protecting the anonymity principle even after the First Stage.

***

## 12. Insurance

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0014 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"The Owner shall insure the Competitors' plans/designs from the time when he assumes responsibility for them and for the duration of his responsibility."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


The **insurance obligation rests on the Owner** — not on the Competitor. Once the Owner receives submitted designs, he is responsible for their protection against loss, damage, or theft. The **amount of insurance shall be stated in the Conditions**.

***

## 13. Exhibitions and Entries

After judgment, the Owner has mandatory obligations regarding public exhibition:

- **All designs — including disqualified entries — must be exhibited** for at least **two (2) weeks**, together with a copy of the signed Jury report
- The exhibition **shall be open to the public free of charge**
- The Owner shall notify **all registered Competitors** in a timely manner of the date, place, and results of the public exhibition, and send them a copy of the Jury's report
- The Owner shall similarly inform the **IAPOA**; photographs of the prize-winning designs shall be sent to the IAPOA with an option for publication

The mandatory exhibition of all entries — including disqualified ones — serves the profession's institutional interest in transparency and public architectural discourse.

***

## 14. Return of Projects

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0015 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"All drawings and plans, other than those which have received prizes or have been purchased and are retained by the Owner, shall be destroyed at the end of the public exhibition, unless provisions are made to the contrary in the Conditions for the ADC."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0016 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Entry Category | Post-Exhibition Disposition | |---|---| | **Prize-winning designs** | Retained by the Owner | | **Purchased designs** | Retained by the Owner | | **All other designs** | **Destroyed** at end of public exhibition, unless Conditions state otherwise | | **Models** | Returned to the Author at the **expense of the Owner** within **one month** of the close of the public exhibition |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## 15. Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) or Litigation

SPP 208 mandates a structured ADR-first dispute resolution framework grounded in **Republic Act No. 9285** (the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act of 2004):

### 15.1 ADR Mandatory in Conditions

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0017 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"Since no regulations, however well drawn up, can preclude the possibility of dispute, provisions for conciliation, mediation and arbitration — i.e. ADR modes under R.A. No. 9285 — must be included in the ADC Conditions and must precede any form of litigation."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


ADR is not optional — it is a mandatory clause that must be included in every ADC's Conditions.

### 15.2 Jury as Sole Arbiters During the Competition

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0018 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"The Jury members are the sole arbiters at all stages, up to the final prize-giving."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


During the adjudication process itself, the Jury's authority is absolute — no external party (not even the IAPOA) can override the Jury's decisions during the competition.

### 15.3 Post-Competition Disputes

For disputes **not related to the adjudication process or awarding of prizes**, the matter shall be settled by **an arbitration process approved by the IAPOA**, without initial recourse to any form of litigation.

### 15.4 Costs

The expenses resulting from any conciliation, mediation, or arbitration procedure shall be **shared equally by the two interested parties** to the ADR proceeding.

***

## 16. ADC Classification Matrix

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0019 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Dimension | Types | |---|---| | **By Purpose** | Project ADC; Ideas Competition | | **By Stage** | Single-Stage; Two-Stage | | **By Openness** | Open; Limited by Invitation | | **By Complexity** | Per SPP 202 Project Groups 1–10 | | **Possible Combinations** | Open Single-Stage Project ADC; Limited Two-Stage Project ADC; Open Ideas Competition; etc. |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## 17. Summary of Owner Obligations

SPP 208 places extensive mandatory obligations on the Owner:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0020 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Obligation | Rule | |---|---| | Obtain IAPOA approval before announcement | Section 3.1 | | Appoint and pay Professional Advisor approved by IAPOA | Section 5.1 | | Appoint Jury and pay all Jury fees, travel, and subsistence | Sections 6.2, 6.13 | | Ensure identical Conditions for all Competitors | Section 4.2 | | Insure all submitted designs | Section 11.1 | | Pay prizes within 1 month of announcement | Section 8.3 | | Pay honoraria to Limited ADC invitees | Section 8.4 | | Pay honoraria to 2
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## 18. Practical Notes for Owners and Competitors

**For Owners:**

- The **IAPOA ADC Committee** is not merely an approving body — it is an active partner in ensuring the competition's fairness and credibility. Engage the IAPOA early in the planning stage, not after the Conditions have been drafted.
- The **first-prize–commission obligation** (Section 8.7) is non-negotiable. An Owner who organizes a Project ADC without intending to build or commission the winner is abusing the competition system — SPP 208 and R.A. 9266 both protect the winner's right to the commission.
- The **12-month rule** (Section 8.8) means that project delays or budget uncertainties do not relieve the Owner of financial obligations to the winning Architect — either commission the project or pay the additional prize sum.

**For Competitors:**

- **Registration = contractual acceptance**. Before registering, review the Conditions carefully — registration is a binding commitment to abide by all ADC rules, including the anonymity requirement.
- **Copyright is retained unconditionally** — submitting an entry does not transfer any ownership rights to the Owner. If the Owner requests to use a non-winning entry, the Competitor may negotiate terms independently.
- In **Limited ADCs by Invitation**, participants are entitled to an honorarium regardless of whether they win a prize — this is separate from prize money and must be claimed.
- In **two-stage competitions**, if selected to proceed to the Second Stage, a separate honorarium is owed for the additional work — ensure this amount is clearly stated in the Conditions before accepting the invitation to the Second Stage.

---



---

## Exam Tip

LEA Trap: Competition types: (1) OPEN = any qualified architect, (2) INVITED = selected architects only, (3) LIMITED = pre-qualified firms, (4) STUDENT = architecture students. Jury = 5 members minimum (majority must be architects). Winner gets: (a) cash prize OR (b) commission. The architect RETAINS copyright of competition entries (unless the contract specifically transfers it).

## Cross‑References

**Spp Doc 207 Design Build Services**, **Spp Doc 209 Architectural Consulting Services Pacs**, **Spp Doc 202 Regular Design Services**, **Uap Spp Doc Standards Of Professional Practice For Philippine Architects**

# SPP Document 201: Standards of Professional Practice on Pre-Design Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 201: Standards of Professional Practice on Pre-Design Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 201** governs the **Pre-Design Services** of Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) in the Philippines. It is part of the 2010 Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), approved on 27 July 2010 as the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266**, known as "The Architecture Act of 2004." It replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 201**, which referred to these non-creative early-stage services under the mnemonic "EPASSSSP" (Economic Feasibility Studies, Project Financing, Architectural Programming, Site Selection & Analysis, Site Utilization & Land Use Studies, Space/Management Studies, and Promotional Services).

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the scope, deliverables, and compensation method for SPP Doc 201 Pre-Design Services: the six pre-design phases (project definition, feasibility studies, site analysis, space programming, design guidelines, and consultant selection); the per-diem or fixed-fee compensation basis; and distinguish pre-design services from regular design services under SPP 202.
---
Pre-Design Services are fundamentally different from design and construction services. They involve **no design or construction work**; instead, they provide the analytical and informational foundation upon which design decisions will later be made. For this reason, they are frequently described as **non-creative work**, and their compensation follows cost-based methods (such as MDPE) rather than percentage-of-construction-cost methods used in SPP Document 202.

***

## Legal and Regulatory Basis

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="authority", title="Legal Authority: R.A. No. 9266 — The Architecture Act of 2004"
- Text: This SPP document is promulgated as part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266**, approved 27 July 2010. Compliance is mandatory for all Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) and Architectural Firms (AFs) in the Philippines.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

SPP Document 201 is promulgated as part of the IRR of R.A. No. 9266, making its observance **mandatory for all Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs)** in the Philippines. Only an RLA — a natural person with a valid PRC Certificate of Registration and a renewable 3-year Professional Identification Card — may legally render pre-design services.

An **Architectural Firm (AF)** may also render these services, provided it is registered with the DTI (as a sole proprietorship) or with the SEC and PRC (as a professional partnership or architectural corporation), in full compliance with Sec. 37 of R.A. No. 9266. Foreign architects wishing to provide pre-design services in the Philippines for projects on Philippine soil must secure a **Temporary/Special Permit (TSP)** from the PRC and a work permit from the **Department of Labor and Employment (DoLE)**, and must work in collaboration with a local RLA.

***

## Why Engage an Architect Early?

The SPP explicitly states that it is **most advantageous to the Client to involve the Architect in the earliest stages of the project**. An experienced architect can provide the client with:

- **Objective project analysis** — independent of any contractor, supplier, or financier
- **Optimization of building needs** against available resources and constraints
- **Early identification of risks**, feasibility gaps, or regulatory hurdles
- **Informed decision-making** before large capital expenditures are committed to design or construction

Because pre-design services determine whether a project is viable at all, engaging an architect at this stage often prevents costly mistakes in later phases.

***

## Scope of Pre-Design Services

The Pre-Design Services cover **a broad line of architectural services ranging from initial problem identification** to activities that allow the Architect to initially conceptualize an array of architectural and allied solutions. The complete list of services nominally included under SPP Document 201 is as follows:

### 2.1 Consultation

When a Client calls upon the Architect to give **oral or written advice and direction**, to attend conferences, or to make evaluations and appraisals regarding a contemplated project and similar activities, the Architect renders valuable inputs **whether or not the Client ultimately pursues the project**. This service covers the broadest and most preliminary stage of client-architect engagement.

### 2.2 Pre-Feasibility Studies

These preliminary studies involve the **procurement, analysis, and use of secondary information** gathered for the project to aid the Client in early decision-making. They represent the Architect's initial assessment of a project's soundness, allowing the Client to promptly explore available or readily identifiable directions and options. **Researched, processed, and validated secondary data** (e.g., electronic sources, print references, statistics) are generally used for such studies — no primary data gathering is required at this stage.

### 2.3 Feasibility Studies

Detailed analysis of the project based on pre-feasibility studies to **determine the viability of a proposed development**. The studies set the project against present and future trends to forecast how it will perform over time. This service requires **primary data gathering and analysis** — including market research, surveys, interviews, cost projections, and financial modeling — making it a more comprehensive and resource-intensive undertaking than a pre-feasibility study.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="tip", title="Key Distinction: Pre-Feasibility vs. Feasibility Studies"
- Text: | | Pre-Feasibility Study | Feasibility Study | |---|---|---| | **Data type** | Secondary (existing, published) | Primary (gathered specifically for project) | | **Depth** | Preliminary, rapid assessment | Detailed, comprehensive analysis | | **Purpose** | Early go/no-go indication | Full viability determination | | **Cost** | Lower | Higher |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

### 2.4 Site Selection and Analysis

This service entails the **formulation of site criteria**, assistance to the Client in site evaluation, and analysis to **determine the most appropriate site/s** for a proposed project or building program. The architect evaluates multiple candidate locations based on criteria such as accessibility, zoning, utilities, topography, and development potential, then recommends the most suitable option.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: **Note:** Under the 1979 UAP framework, Site Selection and Analysis required the involvement of a licensed **Environmental Planner (EnP)** for certain project types. This requirement persists under applicable environmental and land-use laws.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

### 2.5 Site Utilization and Land-Use Studies

The detailed analysis of the site involves the **identification of a site's development potentials** through the proper utilization of land. The analysis covers:

- The context of the site and its surrounding environment
- **Development controls** that apply to the site and its environs (e.g., zoning ordinances, floor-area ratios, setback requirements, easements)

This service determines **how much of the site can be developed**, in what configuration, and subject to what regulatory constraints — information essential for programming, massing, and project costing.

### 2.6 Architectural Research

Architectural research entails the **conduct of primary and secondary researches** to assemble facts used as a basis for conclusions. This may include benchmarking comparable projects, reviewing regulatory requirements, investigating building typologies, or analyzing construction industry trends as they pertain to the project at hand.

### 2.7 Architectural Programming

This is an **analytical problem-seeking process** that leads to the statement and identification of both horizontal and vertical requirements in offering a solution. It incorporates a **space program** with characterizations of the envisioned spaces — such as ambiance, cost range, functional relationships, and performance requirements.

Architectural programming is the bridge between the client's organizational needs and the physical building. Its output (the Program of Requirements or POR) becomes the primary reference document for the architect in SPP 202 Regular Design Services.

### 2.8 Space Planning

The Architect determines the **adequate size and appropriate configuration and assemblage** for a proposed project, considering the use, allocation, and interface of spaces for given activities. Space planning is done mainly through **primary data gathering**, such as:

- Interviews
- Consultations
- Interfaces and focus group discussions (FGDs)
- Space planning surveys
- Space audits

Subsequent analyses include **spatial layouts with stacking concepts**, particularly for multi-storey structures.

### 2.9 Space Management Studies

An analysis of the **space requirements of the project based on organizational structure and functional set-up**, pinpointing linkages and interaction of spaces. The formulation of the space program resulting from this study serves as the basis for the development of the architectural plan/design. While similar to space planning, space management studies focus more on **organizational flow** and departmental relationships, while space planning focuses on the physical dimensions and configurations.

### 2.10 Value Management

This technique is applied in the **cost management process to minimize the negative effect of simplified operations** associated with many cost-reduction programs. The goal of value management is to achieve an **unimpaired program at minimum cost** — meaning that a plan, design, or system that has been successfully value-managed will still satisfy the same performance criteria as costlier alternatives. This is distinct from mere cost-cutting, which may compromise function or quality.

### 2.11 Design Brief Preparation

Under design brief preparation, the Architect states the **project terms of reference (ToR)**, including the concept, objectives, and other necessary requirements to **bid out architectural services** — whether for public or private sector projects. This document, once complete, becomes the basis for inviting and evaluating other architectural firms for comparative selection, as described in SPP Annex "A."

### 2.12 Promotional Services

Projects may require promotional activities in order to **develop and generate financial support and acceptance** from governing agencies or from the general public. In such cases, the Architect acts as the **agent of the Owner**, producing and coordinating the additional activities necessary to complete the services. Throughout such activities, the Architect must maintain professional status as the representative of the Owner.

***

***

## Manner of Providing Services

### Proposal Submission

After the initial meeting, conversation, or correspondence with the Client, **the Architect must submit a written proposal for pre-design services** stating the following:

1. **Scope of Work** — clearly identifying which pre-design services will be rendered
2. **Manner of Payment** — specifying the compensation method and schedule
3. **Owner's Responsibilities** — what the client must provide (data, access, information, approvals)
4. **Other Conditions of Services** — timelines, confidentiality, use of outputs, etc.

### How Services Are Delivered

The architect may render pre-design services in any of the following three ways:

**3.2.1 As an Individual Architect**
The architect must have special training and be knowledgeable in different fields to supplement his or her skills. This is appropriate for smaller, less complex pre-design engagements.

**3.2.2 Architect's Own Staff**
Architects working within a single firm may specialize in different aspects of pre-design — research, programming, spatial analysis — without losing the generalist orientation of the firm. This is suitable for medium to large-scale pre-design engagements.

**3.2.3 By Association, Consultation, or Networking**
Consultation between the Architect and firms of other disciplines (e.g., economists, environmental planners, market researchers) under the **extended terms of the Owner-Architect Agreement** is a common practice for complex, multi-sector pre-design work. The architect remains the lead professional and coordinator of all inputs.

***

## Method of Compensation

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="lea-watch"
- Text: Pre-Design Services use **cost-based methods** (MDPE, Lump Sum, Per Diem) — NOT percentage of Project Construction Cost (PCC). PCC doesn't exist yet at this stage. The LEA frequently tests whether candidates know which documents use PCC vs. cost-based fees.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The Architect's compensation for Pre-Design Services is based on the architect's or firm's **tleants, skill, experience, imagination, and the type and level of professional services provided**. Unlike SPP 202 Regular Design Services, **Pre-Design Services do not use a percentage of Project Construction Cost (PCC)** as a compensation basis, because there is no project construction cost established at this stage.

Compensation for Pre-Design Services may be based on one or more of the following five methods:

***

### Method 1: Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses (MDPE)

The **most commonly used method for pre-design services**. It is a cost-based method applicable to non-creative work such as accounting, secretarial services, research, data gathering, and preparation of reports. This method does not account for creative work, since the value of creative design cannot be measured by time spent.

**Formula:**

Let:

- \(A\) = Architect's rate per hour
- \(C\) = Consultant's rate per hour
- \(T\) = Rate per hour of Technical Staff, Researchers, and others
- \(AN\), \(CN\), \(TN\) = Number of hours spent by Architect, Consultants, and Technical Staff respectively
- \(M\) = Multiplier to account for overhead and reasonable profit (ranges from **1.5 to 2.5**)
- \(R\) = Reimbursable expenses

\[
\text\{Direct Cost\} = (A \times AN) + (C \times CN) + (T \times TN)
\]

\[
\text\{Fee\} = \text\{Direct Cost\} \times M
\]

\[
\text\{Total Cost to Client\} = \text\{Fee\} + R
\]

The multiplier M (ranging from 1.5 to 2.5) depends on the **office set-up, overhead, and experience of the Architect**, and the **complexity of the project**.

**Reimbursable Expenses (R) include:**
- Transportation, living, and housing allowances for foreign consultants
- Out-of-town living and housing allowances for local consultants and technical staff **assigned to places over 100 km** from the architect's area of operation
- Cost of printing extra sets of drawings, reports, maps, and contract documents over the five copies submitted to the Client
- Overseas and long-distance calls
- Technical and laboratory tests, licenses, fees, and taxes

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: The architect must disclose to the client, **at the start of the commission**, the rates of professionals and personnel assigned to the project and the multiplier to be applied, before agreeing on this compensation method.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

### Method 2: Professional Fee Plus Expenses

This method is frequently used **where there is a continuing relationship** involving a series of projects. It establishes a **fixed sum over and above the reimbursement** for the Architect's technical time and overhead. An agreement on the general scope of work is necessary to set an equitable fee.

***

### Method 3: Lump Sum or Fixed Fee

This method may be applied to **government projects**, since they entail more paperwork and time-consuming processes. The fee is agreed upon upfront as a single fixed amount for the defined scope of work. This method provides certainty for both parties but requires that the scope be clearly defined at the outset.

***

### Method 4: Per Diem, Honorarium Plus Reimbursable Expenses

In cases where a Client requests an architect to perform work requiring personal time — such as:

- Attending project-related meetings, conferences, or trips
- Conducting ocular inspection of possible project sites
- Conferring with others regarding prospective investments or ventures

For these activities, the architect (acting as agent of the Owner) may be paid on a **per diem and honorarium basis**, plus **out-of-pocket expenses** such as travel, accommodations, and subsistence.

***

### Method 5: Mixed Methods of Compensation

The SPP provides for **more than one method of compensation** on a project. Each project should be examined to determine the most appropriate and equitable method, and it is common for a complex pre-design engagement to combine, for example, MDPE for research phases and a lump sum for the feasibility report.

***

### Compensation Methods at a Glance

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Relationship to Other SPP Documents

SPP 201 Pre-Design Services operates as the **first stage of the Spectrum of Architectural Services** defined across the SPP framework.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Stage | SPP Document | Feeds Into | |---|---|---| | Pre-Design | **SPP Doc. 201** | SPP Doc. 202 (design) | | Regular Design | SPP Doc. 202 | SPP Doc. 204-A/B (construction) | | Specialized Design | SPP Doc. 203 | SPP Doc. 202 / 204 | | Construction Supervision | SPP Doc. 204-A/B | SPP Doc. 205 | | Post-Construction | SPP Doc. 205 | Long-term building operation | | All Services Combined | SPP Doc. 206 | — |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The outputs of SPP 201 — particularly the feasibility studies, site analysis, and architectural program — form the **primary inputs to the Project Definition Phase of SPP 202**. Without sound pre-design work, the architect entering the design phase lacks the data needed to produce a viable, cost-appropriate, and regulatory-compliant building design.

When a project requires Comprehensive Architectural Services under **SPP Doc. 206**, Pre-Design Services are already included as the first component of that full-service package.

***

## Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**
- Always formalize pre-design engagements with a written proposal even for seemingly minor consultations, as the Architect's time and expertise have professional and commercial value regardless of whether the client proceeds.
- Clearly distinguish **pre-feasibility** (secondary data, lower cost, faster) from **feasibility** (primary data, higher cost, comprehensive) in proposals, since clients often conflate the two.
- The MDPE multiplier (1.5–2.5) must be disclosed upfront; never apply a multiplier without the client's prior agreement.
- Pre-design services are **not covered by the building permit** process; they are entirely contractual between the architect and the client.

**For Clients / Project Proponents:**
- Engaging an RLA for pre-design services — especially feasibility studies and site analysis — before committing to land purchase or project financing is best practice and can prevent costly errors.
- Owners must understand that they are responsible for providing the architect with access to data, documents, and the project site as part of their obligations under the Owner-Architect Agreement.
- Outputs (reports, studies, design briefs) produced under SPP 201 are the **intellectual property of the Architect** under Sec. 33 of R.A. No. 9266 and must not be reproduced or used without authorization.

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Trap: SPP 201 = PRE-design services (before SPP 202). Six phases: (1) Project Definition, (2) Feasibility Study, (3) Site Analysis, (4) Space Programming, (5) Design Guidelines, (6) Consultant Selection. Compensation is per-diem or fixed fee — NOT percentage of construction cost. The most tested distinction: SPP 201 is optional/separate, SPP 202 is the standard.

# SPP Document 204-B: Standards of Professional Practice on Construction Management Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 204-B: Standards of Professional Practice on Construction Management Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 204-B** governs **Construction Management (CM) Services** — a broader, more managerial form of construction oversight that goes beyond the on-site inspection duties of the Construction Supervision Group (CSG) under SPP 204-A. It is part of the 2010 Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), promulgated as the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004), and replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 204-B**.

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the scope of SPP Doc 204-B Construction Management Services — cost control, schedule management, contract administration, coordination of multiple contractors, value engineering, and project close-out — and distinguish CM from full-time supervision (CM manages the entire construction process including cost and schedule, not just quality and conformance); apply the percentage-of-construction-cost compensation.
---
Where SPP 204-A focuses on **on-site quality control and inspection**, SPP 204-B positions the Construction Manager (CM) as the **owner's primary point of accountability for the entire construction process** — covering programming, coordination of all parties, cost control, time management, and quality assurance from a project-wide management perspective. Construction Management Services arose in response to the increasing complexity of construction projects and the corresponding demand for more effective cost control and faster project implementation consistent with high quality of work.

***

## Legal and Regulatory Basis

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="authority", title="Legal Authority: R.A. No. 9266 — The Architecture Act of 2004"
- Text: This SPP document is promulgated as part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266**, approved 27 July 2010. Compliance is mandatory for all Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) and Architectural Firms (AFs) in the Philippines.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

SPP 204-B is promulgated as part of the IRR of R.A. No. 9266. The Construction Manager must be a **State-regulated professional** — preferably a **Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA)** with managerial capabilities and extensive experience in the field of construction. Since construction management is **not part of the regular services of the Architect** under SPP 202, the services rendered by the Architect as Construction Manager shall be **separately compensated**.

***

## Background: Why Construction Management Was Instituted

Due to the increasing complexity of construction projects, the construction industry faced two key pressures:

1. **The need for more effective cost control** — Large and multi-phase projects require systematic tracking of budgets, procurement, and change orders beyond what periodic site visits can address
2. **The need for faster project implementation** — Tight schedules and multi-contractor environments require proactive coordination rather than reactive inspection

Construction Management Services were instituted to fill this gap — bridging the owner's expectations of on-time, on-budget, quality construction with the operational realities of managing complex projects.

***

## Who May Serve as Construction Manager

The Construction Manager (CM) may be:

1. **A member of the Owner's own staff** — an in-house professional hired directly by the owner's organization
2. **An independent individual** — a sole practitioner hired specifically for the project
3. **A firm** — a construction management company hired by the owner

An **Architect** is explicitly recognized as a suitable CM. The architect's training in coordinating various specialties — structural, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, interiors, and site development — allows the architect to supervise and assure proper monitoring of all construction activities with respect to quality, workmanship, and cost.

Architects who are also contractors, or who have been in responsible charge of construction works, are considered **especially capable of becoming Construction Managers**. This practical construction background, combined with professional design education, makes the architect uniquely qualified for the CM role.

***

## Functions and Description of Tasks

The responsibilities of the Construction Manager (CM) **include all the functions of the Construction Supervision Group (CSG)** as defined under SPP 204-A, plus broader management responsibilities. The four core CM functions are:

### 2.1 Coordination and Supervision

The CM coordinates all parties involved in the construction project — owner, architect-of-record, engineers, specialist consultants, contractors, sub-contractors, and suppliers. Coordination activities include:

- **Pre-Construction Phase**: Regular consultations with the Owner, Architects, and Engineers on all aspects of project planning — during and concurrent with the design development phase
- **Scheduling**: Preparation and monitoring of the overall project implementation schedule, including sequencing of all major trades
- **Interface Management**: Ensuring that the work of different contractors and sub-contractors does not conflict in terms of sequence, access, space, or systems
- **Meeting Facilitation**: Convening and minuting all construction coordination meetings, progress review sessions, and technical workshops
- **Procurement Coordination**: Assisting the owner in pre-qualifying contractors, evaluating bids, and recommending awards

### 2.2 Cost and Time Control

The CM is the owner's primary safeguard against cost overruns and schedule delays. Cost and time control activities include:

- **Budget Monitoring**: Tracking actual expenditures against the approved project budget and the Statement of Probable Project Construction Cost (SPPCC)
- **Change Order Management**: Evaluating all proposed changes, their cost implications, and schedule impacts before submission to the owner for approval
- **Progress Billing Review**: Reviewing and verifying contractor payment applications against actual work accomplished
- **Forecasting**: Providing the owner with regular updated forecasts of final project cost and completion date
- **Schedule Recovery**: Identifying and recommending corrective actions when work falls behind the approved program

### 2.3 Quality Control of Work

While the CSG handles day-to-day field quality control, the CM provides a higher-level quality assurance function:

- **QCP Oversight**: Reviewing and approving the Quality Control Plan (QCP) of the CSG
- **Material and Equipment Approval**: Coordinating the review and approval of material submittals, shop drawings, and equipment specifications
- **Inspection Coordination**: Scheduling and coordinating third-party testing and inspections (soil testing, concrete testing, etc.)
- **Non-Conformance Management**: Reviewing and dispositioning non-conformance reports from the CSG
- **Commissioning Coordination**: Overseeing the commissioning and testing of all building systems prior to turnover

### 2.4 Keeping of Records

The CM maintains comprehensive project records covering all management activities:

- **Project files** — all contracts, purchase orders, correspondence, and approvals
- **Progress reports** — weekly and monthly reports to the owner covering cost, schedule, and quality status
- **Meeting minutes** — records of all coordination, progress, and technical meetings
- **Change order log** — chronological record of all approved and pending changes
- **Procurement log** — status of all material and equipment procurement
- **As-built documentation** — coordination of final as-built drawings and warranties for turnover

***

### CM Functions at a Glance

- Text: | Function | Core Activities | Who Benefits | |---|---|---| | **Coordination and Supervision** | All-party coordination, scheduling, interface management, procurement | Owner, Architect, Engineers | | **Cost and Time Control** | Budget tracking, change order management, billing review, forecasting | Owner | | **Quality Control of Work** | QCP oversight, submittals, testing, commissioning | Owner, End Users | | **Keeping of Records** | Files, progress reports, meeting minutes, change logs, as-bui
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## The CM and the CSG: How They Relate

A critical clarification in SPP 204-B is the relationship between the **Construction Manager (CM)** and the **Construction Supervision Group (CSG)**:

- The CM's responsibilities **include** the CSG's functions — meaning CM services are a **superset** of CSG services
- The CM may **hire the CSG to be under his employ**, directly managing and compensating the CSG team
- Alternatively, the CM may **supervise the CSG hired directly by the Owner**

This dual arrangement allows flexibility: the owner may prefer to hire and pay the CSG directly (for accountability and cost transparency), while still placing the CSG under the CM's technical and managerial direction.

***

## Limitation of Authority

The SPP explicitly limits the CM's authority to prevent liability overreach and protect the integrity of both the design and the construction contract:

**The Architect as CM shall NOT:**

1. **Involve directly with the Contractor's work** in such a way that it may be construed that the CM is assuming the Contractor's liability as provided for under **Article 1723 of the Civil Code** — meaning the CM must not direct, supervise, or control the contractor's construction methods to the point where the CM could be held solidarily liable for structural defects

2. **Impose methods, systems, or designs** that will substantially affect the construction schedule or **impair the design concept of the Architect-of-record** — this preserves the design integrity of the Aor and prevents the CM from effectively re-designing the project through construction directives

These limitations are analogous to those of the CSG under SPP 204-A, but are expressed at the management level rather than the field level.

***

## Legal Responsibility

SPP 204-B draws a clear and important distinction between the CM's **scope of responsibility** and the **limits of liability**:

### 4.1 Direct Responsibility to the Owner

The Architect as CM is **directly responsible to the Owner** on all aspects of construction work:
- Programming
- Coordination
- Quality control
- Cost control
- Time management

This direct responsibility is broader than the CSG's field-level accountability — the CM answers for the entire management process, not just on-site inspection.

### 4.2 Limits of CM Liability

The CM **assumes no liability** for equipment failure or structural collapse under two specific conditions:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Condition | Liability Exclusion | |---|---| | Equipment failure or building collapse due to **deficiencies in the plan/design** | CM is NOT liable, **provided the CM did not participate in the plan/design review and approval** | | Equipment failure or building collapse due to **deficiencies in the manner of construction** | CM is NOT liable, **provided the CM faithfully discharged his functions during construction/project implementation** |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

These liability exclusions incentivize the CM to faithfully perform supervision duties (condition 2) while also staying out of design review (condition 1), unless separately retained as the Aor or design consultant. When the CM also serves as Aor, condition 1 no longer applies, and the CM-Aor faces full exposure under Article 1723 of the Civil Code.

***

## Qualifications

The Construction Manager may be an individual or a firm. The required qualifications are:

1. **State-regulated professional** — The individual or the principal of the firm must be a licensed professional under Philippine law; being an RLA (Registered and Licensed Architect) is the preferred qualification
2. **Managerial capabilities** — The CM must demonstrate organizational and managerial competence in coordinating multi-discipline construction teams
3. **Extensive experience in construction** — Practical exposure to construction processes, materials, systems, sequencing, and contracting is essential

The SPP notes that **architects who are also contractors, or who have been in responsible charge of construction works, are usually capable of becoming Construction Managers** — because such individuals combine design understanding with operational construction knowledge.

***

## Method of Compensation

Since construction management is not part of the architect's regular services under SPP 202, CM services are **always separately compensated**. The same six methods applicable to SPP 204-A apply here:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Method | Best Used For | Key Feature | |---|---|---| | **% of Project Construction Cost (PCC)** | All regular construction projects | Separate from SPP 202 design fee | | **MDPE** | Variable-scope management work | Multiplier 1.5–2.5 on personnel hours | | **Professional Fee + Expenses** | Ongoing/repeat client relationships | Fixed sum + reimbursements | | **Lump Sum / Fixed Fee** | Government projects; well-defined scope | Predictable total cost | | **Per Diem + Honorarium** | Short or limit
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The specific percentage rates for CM services under the PCC method are prescribed in the **Architect's Guidelines** and are distinct from — and in addition to — the fees for SPP 202 design services and SPP 204-A supervision services.

***

## SPP 204-A vs. SPP 204-B: Key Distinctions

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | | SPP 204-A (Fulltime Supervision) | SPP 204-B (Construction Management) | |---|---|---| | **Primary Role** | On-site inspection and quality control | Project-wide management of cost, time, quality, and coordination | | **Scope** | CSG tasks: QC, evaluation, daily reports, filing | All CSG tasks + coordination, cost/time control, broader record keeping | | **Personnel** | CSG — qualified architects on-site daily | CM — senior professional overseeing the CSG and all parties | | **Reporting** | 
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## SPP 204-B and Project Management (PM) under SPP 206

When an architect is hired to provide **Comprehensive Architectural Services (CAS)** under SPP 206, the architect assumes both the role of **Project Manager (PM)** and **Construction Manager (CM)**. In this context:

- **Project Management (PM)** refers to management activities **over and above** normal architectural and engineering (A&E) services, carried out across all phases — pre-design, design, and construction
- The PM oversees time, cost, and quality relative to the construction of the project
- The **presence of a Project Manager does not relieve the designers and contractors** of their respective normal duties and responsibilities
- If the PM also serves as CM to oversee time, cost, and quality control during construction, the PM shall provide the services detailed under SPP Documents 204-A and/or 204-B

The PM fee under SPP 206 is generally **2–5% of the Estimated Project Cost**, using combination methods; if the PM also performs regular architectural services for the same project, those are compensated separately under SPP 202.

***

## Relationship to Other SPP Documents

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | SPP Document | Relationship | |---|---| | **SPP Doc. 202** (Regular Design Services) | SPP 202 covers only periodic construction phase visits; SPP 204-B provides the full management overlay | | **SPP Doc. 204-A** (Fulltime Supervision) | SPP 204-B subsumes all of 204-A's CSG functions plus adds broader management responsibilities | | **SPP Doc. 205** (Post-Construction) | After project turnover, SPP 205 post-construction services take over from the CM's construction-phase role | | **SPP Doc. 2
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**
- Never combine the Aor and CM roles without a clearly written, separately compensated agreement — doing so increases exposure to solidary liability under Article 1723 of the Civil Code, since both design deficiencies and construction deficiencies may now be attributable to the same professional.
- The CM role requires genuine managerial competence — scheduling, cost reporting, contract administration, and stakeholder management — beyond what most design-track architects practice. Consider supplementing with a formal project management credential or partnering with an experienced CM firm.
- Keep the CM's management records meticulously. The liability exclusion under SPP 204-B Sec. 4.2 is conditioned on the CM having "faithfully discharged his functions" — contemporaneous documentation is the primary evidence of faithful discharge.

**For Clients / Project Proponents:**
- Engaging a CM under SPP 204-B is most valuable for **large, multi-phase, or multi-contractor projects** where the owner's in-house team lacks the capacity to coordinate all parties directly.
- The CM fee is a **separate cost** from the architect's SPP 202 design fee and the CSG's SPP 204-A supervision fee — budget for all three independently.
- Specify in the Owner-CM Agreement whether the CM will directly hire and pay the CSG, or whether the owner will hire the CSG separately with the CM providing technical oversight — the two arrangements have different billing and accountability implications.

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Trap: CM (204-B) vs Full-Time Supervision (204-A): CM manages COST and SCHEDULE in addition to quality. CM coordinates MULTIPLE prime contractors. CM produces (1) CPM schedule, (2) Cost reports, (3) Change order management, (4) Value engineering options. The key test point: CM has authority over budget, FTS does not.



---

CM produces (1) CPM schedule, (2) Cost reports, (3) Change order management, (4) Value engineering options. The key test point: CM has authority over budget, FTS does not.
