proposed_content:
# SPP Document 206: Standards of Professional Practice on Comprehensive Architectural Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 206: Standards of Professional Practice on Comprehensive Architectural Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 206** governs **Comprehensive Architectural Services (CAS)** — the broadest and most integrative SPP document in the entire 2010 series. It replaces the **1979 UAP Doc. 206** and forms part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004).

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the scope of SPP Doc 206 Comprehensive Architectural Services — the full spectrum of pre-design through post-construction services combined into a single commission; explain how the 15% ceiling on basic fee for comprehensive services is calculated; determine when a comprehensive service agreement is appropriate vs separate SPP Doc agreements for each phase.
---
SPP 206 is not a standalone service but an **umbrella framework** that consolidates the entire range of services from SPP 201 through SPP 205 under the management of a single professional — the **Project Manager (PM)**. Understanding SPP 206 requires thorough knowledge of all preceding SPP documents, as CAS is only meaningful when each of its component services is fully understood.

***

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The Evolution of Comprehensive Architectural Services

The concept of Comprehensive Architectural Services **crystallized through the years in response to the demands of emerging complex building projects**. The architectural profession's transition from providing "basic" and "additional" services to services of a comprehensive nature came from a critical realization: **continuity of services related to design and construction is necessary for the execution of a completely viable project**.

In this extended dimension, **the Architect is the prime professional** — functioning as creator, author, and coordinator of the building design that becomes the basis for construction. The Architect must be knowledgeable in other fields in addition to building design in order to properly assist and serve the Client.

A critical policy principle in SPP 206 is that **the Architect is NOT expected to perform all the services personally**. Rather, the Architect acts as the **agent of the Client** in procuring and coordinating the necessary services required by a project. CAS is not about one person doing everything — it is about one professional orchestrating everything on behalf of the owner.

### 1.2 What is Project Management (PM)?

When the Owner hires an Architect or a firm to **coordinate the whole range of CAS**, this constitutes **Project Management (PM)**. PM is formally defined as:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"Management activities over and above the normal architectural and engineering (A&E) services carried out during the pre-design, design, and construction phase. The overall objective is to have control over time, cost, and quality relative to the construction of a project."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

Three foundational principles govern the PM role:

1. **The PM does NOT relieve designers or contractors** of their respective normal duties and responsibilities in design and construction
2. **The PM complements** the functions of Architects, Engineers, and Contractors in meeting the broad and complex requirements of projects
3. **The PM's primary responsibility** is the exercise of **overall cost control** — planning, programming, and monitoring activities, and advising on material costs and construction methods

***

## 2. Scope of Services

The scope of SPP 206 is the entire continuum of services from SPP 201 through SPP 205, plus a specifically defined PM scope.

### 2.1 Comprehensive Architectural Services

CAS encompasses all five service clusters from the preceding SPP documents:

#### 2.1.1 Pre-Design Services (SPP Doc. 201)

All 12 pre-design services under SPP 201:

- Consultation
- Pre-Feasibility Studies
- Feasibility Studies
- Site Selection and Analysis
- Site Utilization and Land-Use Studies
- Architectural Research
- Architectural Programming
- Space Planning
- Space Management Studies
- Value Management
- Design Brief Preparation
- Promotional Services

#### 2.1.2 Regular Design Services (SPP Doc. 202)

All 6 phases of the regular design service under SPP 202:

- Project Definition Phase
- Schematic Design Phase
- Design Development Phase
- Contract Documents Phase
- Bidding or Negotiation Phase
- Construction Phase

#### 2.1.3 Specialized Architectural Services (SPP Doc. 203)

All 23 specialized services under SPP 203:

- Architectural Interiors (AI)
- Acoustic Design
- Architectural Lighting Layout and Design
- Site Development Planning (SDP)
- Site and Physical Planning Services (including Master Development Planning, Subdivision Planning, and Urban Design)
- Comprehensive Development Planning (CDP)
- Historic and Cultural Heritage Conservation and Planning
- Security Evaluation and Planning
- Building Systems Design
- Facilities Maintenance Support
- Building Testing and Commissioning
- Building Environmental Certification
- Forensic Architecture
- Building Appraisal
- Structural Conceptualization
- Preliminary Services
- Contract Documentation and Review
- Post-Design Services (including Construction Management Services)
- Dispute Avoidance and Resolution
- Architectural Research Methods
- Special Building/Facility Planning and Design
- Building Components
- Management of Architectural Practices

#### 2.1.4 Construction Services (SPP Docs. 204-A and 204-B)

- Fulltime Supervision Services (SPP Document 204-A)
- Construction Management Services (SPP Document 204-B)

#### 2.1.5 Post-Construction Services (SPP Doc. 205)

- Building and Facilities Administration
- Post-Construction Evaluation

***

### 2.2 Project Management Scope

In addition to coordinating all CAS services, the PM has a specifically defined management scope across two phases:

#### Pre-Construction Phase

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"As early as during the design development phase, perhaps even concurrently with the Architect's commission, the Project Manager (PM) should conduct regular consultations with the Owner and with the Architects and Engineers (for A&E services) on all aspects of planning for the project."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

This means the PM's engagement begins **before construction starts** — ideally during the design development stage — so that programming, procurement planning, budget controls, and contractor pre-qualification are all in place before the project goes to bid.

#### Construction Phase

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"If the Project Manager (PM) also serves as the Construction Manager (CM) to oversee time, cost, and quality control during the construction of the project, he shall provide the services detailed under SPP Documents 204-A and/or 204-B."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The PM's default role during construction is **coordination and oversight**. If the PM also takes on the CM role, the full SPP 204-A/204-B scope applies and additional compensation is owed.

***

### CAS Full Scope at a Glance

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | SPP Document | Service Cluster | Sub-Services | |---|---|---| | SPP 201 | Pre-Design | 12 services | | SPP 202 | Regular Design | 6 phases | | SPP 203 | Specialized Services | 23 services | | SPP 204-A | Fulltime Supervision | CSG services | | SPP 204-B | Construction Management | CM services | | SPP 205 | Post-Construction | 2 service clusters | | **SPP 206 (PM layer)** | **Coordination of ALL above** | **Pre-construction + Construction PM** |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## 3. Manner of Providing Services

### 3.1 Comprehensive Architectural Services

The normal engagement model is straightforward: **the Architect enters into a single contract with the Owner** to perform Comprehensive Architectural Services. By the very nature of the CAS contract, the Architect **assumes the dual role of the Project Manager (PM) and the Construction Manager (CM)** — or effectively, the overall coordinator whose functions are outlined under SPP 206.

To perform the variety of CAS services, the Architect **must make full use of his own capability as well as services offered by other professionals**. The Architect may:

1. **Expand his own staff** by hiring the experts needed, or
2. **Form a multi-disciplinary team** consisting of professionals such as (but not limited to):

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Professional Type | Role in CAS Team | |---|---| | Architects | Design, documentation, site supervision | | Engineers | Structural, M/E/P systems design | | Market Analysts | Feasibility and demand studies | | Accountants | Cost tracking and financial reporting | | General Contractors | Construction implementation | | Real Estate Consultants | Site analysis, land use advisory | | Sociologists | Community impact, occupancy behavior | | Planners | Urban design, land use planning | | Bankers | Pr
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

This multi-disciplinary team model is the defining feature of CAS — the Architect as PM does not work alone, but assembles and leads the best team for the specific project.

### 3.2 Project Management (PM)

The PM's organizational relationships under SPP 206 are specifically defined:

#### 3.2.1 PM and the Construction Manager / Fulltime Supervisor

If a PM is hired by the Owner, the PM may:

- **Hire the CM**, with the CM compensated either by the PM directly or by the Owner directly (on salary or percentage of construction cost), OR
- **Serve as the CM himself**, assuming the full SPP 204-B scope

In like manner, the **Fulltime Supervisor (under SPP 204-A)** can either be a staff member of the PM or hired directly by the Owner.

#### 3.2.2 The Owner-Architect-Engineer-Contractor Team

The PM operates as a **member of the Owner-Architect-Engineer-Contractor (OAEC) Team**. In this Team Approach, each member has precedence in their own field of expertise:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Team Member | Primary Responsibility | Authority Domain | |---|---|---| | **Architect & Specialist Consultants** | Prime responsibility for plan/design of the project | Design decisions | | **Engineers** | Responsible for respective engineering plans | Structural, M/E/P design | | **Contractor** | Responsible for men, equipment, and delivery of the project | Construction methods | | **Owner** | Makes decisions on the project; assures funds are available | Final approvals, financing | | **Proje
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The PM sits atop the coordination hierarchy — not as a superior to the designer or contractor in their respective domains, but as the **integrating authority** who ensures all team members deliver on schedule, within budget, and at the required quality level.

***

## 4. Method of Compensation

SPP 206 is notably concise in its compensation provisions — reflecting that the detailed fee schedules are contained in the **Architect's Guidelines** rather than in the SPP text itself.

### 4.1 PM Compensation: Percentage of Project Construction Cost

The primary compensation method for the Project Manager is a **percentage of the Project Construction Cost (PCC)**:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: *"The Project Manager is compensated on a percentage basis, as shall be described in the Architect's Guidelines."*
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The **Recommended Professional Fee (RPF) for Project Management Services is 2% to 5% of the Project Construction Cost (PCC)**. The exact rate within this range depends on:

- The complexity and scale of the project
- Whether the PM also serves as CM and/or CSG
- The extent of specialized services engaged under SPP 203
- The duration of the project lifecycle

### 4.2 Separate Compensation for Design Services

A critical rule: **if the Architect as PM also performs regular design services for the same project, those design services shall be compensated SEPARATELY** as stipulated in SPP Document 202.

This means a PM who also acts as the Aor is entitled to **two separate fees**:
- **PM Fee**: 2–5% of PCC under SPP 206
- **Design Fee**: As per SPP 202 minimum basic fee schedules (% of PCC based on project group)

The two fees are cumulative and are not mutually exclusive.

### 4.3 Additional Compensation Methods

While the percentage method is primary, the Architect's Guidelines also recognize additional methods applicable to CAS/PM services:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Method | Applicability | |---|---| | **Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense (MDPE)** | Variable-scope pre-construction PM activities | | **Professional Fee Plus Expenses (PFPE)** | Ongoing PM engagement with defined deliverables | | **Lump Sum / Fixed Fee** | Government projects; well-defined PM scope |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## 5. CAS vs. Individual SPP Engagements

A critical question in practice is: **when should a client engage CAS under SPP 206 vs. engaging individual SPP 201–205 services separately?**

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Factor | Individual SPP Engagements | Comprehensive Architectural Services (SPP 206) | |---|---|---| | **Project Complexity** | Suitable for straightforward single-phase projects | Best for complex, multi-phase, multi-contractor projects | | **Owner's Capacity** | Owner has staff to coordinate consultants and contractors | Owner lacks capacity for multi-party coordination | | **Continuity** | Multiple separate contracts; risk of coordination gaps | Single contract; PM maintains continuity acro
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The key insight is that **CAS does not replace the individual services** — it adds a management layer on top of them. The total cost of a CAS engagement includes both the individual SPP fees and the PM fee.

***

## 6. CAS and the Architect as Prime Professional

SPP 206 articulates the most complete expression of the **Architect's role as Prime Professional** in the construction process. The three dimensions of this primacy are:

### 6.1 Creator
The Architect conceives the design — translating the Owner's program and vision into spatial, aesthetic, and technical proposals that form the basis for all subsequent work.

### 6.2 Author
The Architect produces the contract documents — drawings, specifications, and reports — that become the legal and technical basis for construction and for all regulatory approvals.

### 6.3 Coordinator
As PM under CAS, the Architect coordinates the entire team — from market analysts and lawyers in the pre-design phase, through engineers and contractors during construction, to maintenance contractors and appraisers in post-construction — ensuring that each specialist's contribution integrates into a coherent, viable project.

This three-dimensional primacy (Creator–Author–Coordinator) is what distinguishes the Architect's CAS role from that of a pure project manager from another profession — the architect brings both the **creative and technical authority** over the design and the **management authority** over the project lifecycle.

***

## 7. Relationship to Other SPP Documents

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0010 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | SPP Document | Nature of Relationship | |---|---| | **SPP 201** (Pre-Design) | First service cluster under CAS; PM engagement should ideally begin at this phase | | **SPP 202** (Regular Design) | Core design service under CAS; Aor-PM earns SPP 202 fee separately | | **SPP 203** (Specialized Services) | 23 specialized services all fall within CAS scope; PM procures and coordinates specialist consultants | | **SPP 204-A** (Fulltime Supervision) | PM may absorb CSG into staff, or coordinate a sep
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## 8. Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**

- The PM fee of **2–5% of PCC** is in addition to — not inclusive of — the SPP 202 design fee and any SPP 203/204/205 specialist fees. The total professional fees on a full CAS project can be substantial; ensure that the owner understands and budgets for the full fee structure before engagement.
- When assembling the CAS team (Section 3.1.2), the Architect as PM should formalize the team structure through **sub-consultancy agreements or joint venture arrangements** — clearly defining scope, fee-sharing, liability, and deliverables for each team member.
- The PM does NOT absorb liability from designers or contractors — each professional retains liability within their own scope. This must be reflected in the Owner-PM agreement and in each sub-consultant agreement to prevent liability ambiguity.

**For Clients / Project Proponents:**

- Engaging an Architect under SPP 206 as PM means **paying two separate fee streams**: the PM coordination fee (2–5% PCC) and the individual SPP 202 design fee (per project group). Clients should request a full fee schedule upfront that itemizes all SPP fees applicable to their project.
- CAS is most valuable for **large, complex, or phased development projects** where the owner cannot effectively coordinate architects, engineers, specialists, contractors, and administrators directly. For a simple residential or small commercial project, engaging all SPP services individually may be more cost-effective.
- The **Owner remains the ultimate decision-maker** even under CAS — the PM advises, coordinates, and manages, but the Owner retains authority over all final approvals and funding decisions. CAS does not transfer project ownership decisions to the PM.

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Trap: Comprehensive = SPP 201 + 202 + 204 + 205 in a single contract. Basic fee = 15% of construction cost (max). Not included: specialized services (203). Comprehensive is a BUNDLE — the 15% ceiling applies to the bundle, not to each phase. The most tested: if a client asks for 'all services', it likely triggers SPP 206 (Comprehensive), not just SPP 202.



---

## Exam Tip

ALE Trap: Comprehensive = SPP 201 + 202 + 204 + 205 in a single contract. Basic fee = 15% of construction cost (max). Not included: specialized services (203). Comprehensive is a BUNDLE — the 15% ceiling applies to the bundle, not to each phase. The most tested: if a client asks for 'all services', it likely triggers SPP 206 (Comprehensive), not just SPP 202.

## Cross‑References

**Spp Doc 201 Pre Design Services**, **Spp Doc 202 Regular Design Services**, **Spp Doc 205 Post Construction Services**, **Spp Doc 207 Design Build Services**

## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Lea Prac Svc 010 Core Concept** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?
## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Describe interior design as an allied architectural service.
- Explain the architect's qualifications for providing interior design services.
- Identify the phases and deliverables of interior design projects.
- Distinguish interior design (architect-led) from interior decoration.

SPP Doc 208 governs Architectural Design Competitions (ADC) — the structured process for selecting exceptional design solutions through competitive evaluation. The LEA tests your knowledge of competition types, the roles of professional advisors and jury members, and the conditions that maintain professional standards throughout the competitive process.

## Core Concept

SPP Doc 208 establishes the framework for organizing and managing architectural design competitions at the professional level. These competitions serve dual purposes: identifying innovative design approaches and developing emerging tleant within the profession. The professional advisor and jury composition determine competition credibility and outcomes.

### Rationale and Classification of Design Competitions

Design competitions emerged from the need to secure superior design solutions without limiting consideration to a single firm. Competitions stimulate creative exploration, elevate design standards, and provide exposure for tleanted architects. SPP Doc 208 classifies competitions into two primary categories: Project Architectural Design Competitions (PADCs) and Ideas Competitions. Project competitions address specific built work with defined sites and detailed briefs. Ideas competitions explore conceptual solutions without immediate construction intent.

### Project Architectural Design Competitions

Project Architectural Design Competitions require complete architectural documentation including drawings, specifications, and technical details. These competitions follow established submission protocols and evaluation criteria defined in the competition brief. Participating architects invest significant resources in design development, research, and visualization. The winning design typically becomes the basis for detailed design and construction administration by the selected firm.

### Ideas Competitions and Emerging Tleant Development

Ideas competitions encourage conceptual exploration without requiring full construction documentation. These competitions lower participation barriers and engage a broader range of practitioners including students and emerging firms. Ideas competitions advance innovative thinking, test new methodologies, and generate design precedents for future projects. Recognition through competition success establishes professional reputation and attracts future commissions.

### Professional Advisor and Technical Advisor Roles

The professional advisor oversees competition administration, ensures compliance with professional standards, and maintains procedural integrity. This role requires extensive knowledge of architectural practice, competition management, and professional ethics. Technical advisors provide specialized expertise in specific design disciplines or sustainability standards. The professional advisor and technical advisors collaborate to ensure evaluation fairness and consistency.

### Jury Composition and Evaluation Standards

Competition juries combine professional architects, consultants, users, and community representatives to ensure diverse perspectives. Jury members evaluate submissions against established criteria including functional performance, innovation, cost efficiency, and constructability. Jury independence protects evaluation integrity and prevents conflicts of interest. Clear evaluation criteria, documented deliberations, and transparent result communication build credibility and professional respect.

### Competition Secretariat and Administrative Functions

The competition secretariat manages submission reception, document organization, confidentiality protocols, and result announcement procedures. This role ensures procedural compliance and protects intellectual property during the evaluation process. The secretariat coordinates between organizers, participants, professional advisors, and jury members. Effective administration supports fair competition and protects all parties' interests.

### Conditions and Professional Standards in Competitions

Competition conditions establish submission requirements, intellectual property rights, compensation for winning and selected designs, and timeline specifications. Professional conditions require truthful representations, ethical conduct, and respect for competitors' intellectual contributions. Conditions address publication rights, exhibition arrangements, and design team acknowledgment. Clear conditions prevent disputes and maintain professional standards throughout the competitive process.

# SPP Document 202: Standards of Professional Practice on Regular Design Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 202: Standards of Professional Practice on Regular Design Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 202** governs the **Regular Design Services** of Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) in the Philippines — the core of architectural practice, covering everything from the first consultation with the client all the way through the turnover of the completed project. It is part of the 2010 Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), promulgated as the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004), and replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 202**.

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the five phases of SPP Doc 202 Regular Design Services (Schematic Design, Design Development, Contract Documents, Bidding Assistance, Construction Administration) and their deliverables, fee percentages, and architect's level of involvement per phase; apply the 20%-30%-50% fee split across SD/DD/CD; and determine when a phase is complete and the next begins.
---
Regular Design Services represent what most people understand as "the architect's job" — translating the client's needs and requirements into physical spaces and forms, preparing all necessary construction documents, managing the bidding or negotiation process, and providing oversight during construction until the project is turned over. SPP 202 is the most frequently referenced document in day-to-day architectural practice because it governs the standard engagement between an architect and a client for any building project.

***

## Legal and Regulatory Basis

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="authority", title="Legal Authority: R.A. No. 9266 — The Architecture Act of 2004"
- Text: This SPP document is promulgated as part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266**, approved 27 July 2010. Compliance is mandatory for all Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) and Architectural Firms (AFs) in the Philippines.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

SPP 202 applies to all **Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs)** — natural persons with valid PRC Certificates of Registration and 3-year renewable Professional Identification Cards. It equally applies to architectural firms (AFs) organized as DTI-registered sole proprietorships, or SEC-registered professional partnerships or corporations, all subject to Sec. 37 of R.A. No. 9266.

**Foreign architects** offering services in the Philippines for projects on Philippine soil must comply with Sec. 38 of R.A. No. 9266, which requires a **Temporary/Special Permit (TSP)** from the PRC and a work permit from the **Department of Labor and Employment (DoLE)**, and must collaborate with a local **Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA)** as a counterpart. **BPO/KPO firms** registered with DTI or SEC to serve overseas clients are not authorized to provide architectural services for projects on Philippine soil unless they are PRC-registered architectural firms satisfying Sec. 37.

***

## The Architect's Role in Regular Practice

In regular practice, the Architect acts as the **Owner's/Client's/Proponent's Adviser and/or Representative**. This dual role means the architect:

- **Translates** the owner's needs and requirements into spaces and forms in the best manner of professional service
- **Starts** work at the inception of the project when the owner outlines requirements
- **Covers** all aspects from analysis and study of needs, to preparation of instruments of service, to supervision during project implementation
- **Ends** work only when the general contractor or builder turns over the completed project to the owner

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: The architect does not guarantee construction costs, nor assume professional responsibility for cost estimates, since the architect has no control over the cost of labor, materials, or the many factors that affect competitive bidding — unless glaring errors or discrepancies are clearly evident.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## Scope of Services: The Six Phases

SPP 202 organizes the architect's services into **six sequential phases**, each with specific deliverables.

### Phase 1: Project Definition Phase

This is the "investigation" stage. The project requirements are defined before any design begins. The architect:

- Consults with the owner to ascertain the **conceptual framework and related requirements** of the project, and confirms these requirements
- Gathers relevant information and data leading to the definition of the project's scope, including the scope of the architect's services
- Reviews and refines the owner's space requirements and **translates them into an architectural program**
- Prepares an **initial Statement of Probable Project Construction Cost (SPPCC)**

The SPPCC is not a fixed guarantee of cost — it is an initial estimate based on available data, subject to refinement in every subsequent phase.

### Phase 2: Schematic Design Phase

Once requirements are defined, the architect moves into conceptual design. The architect:

- **Evaluates** the owner's program, schedule, budget, and project site, and proposes methods of project delivery
- **Prepares the initial line drawings** representing design studies leading to a recommended solution, with a general description of the project for the owner's approval
- **Submits an updated SPPCC** based on current cost parameters

The schematic design output is the first visual representation of the project. Owner approval at this stage is critical before the architect proceeds to the next phase.

### Phase 3: Design Development Phase

Based on approved schematics and conceptual plans, the architect prepares:

- **Design Development documents** — plans, elevations, sections, and other drawings elaborating the approved schematic
- **Outline specifications** — fixing and illustrating the size and character of the entire project as to type of materials, and type of structural, electrical, mechanical, sanitary, electronic, and communications systems
- **Diagrammatic layout** of construction systems
- An **updated SPPCC** for submission to the owner

### Phase 4: Contract Document Phase

Based on approved Design Development documents, the architect:

- Prepares the **complete Contract Documents** — detailed designs and construction drawings setting forth all the work required for architectural, structural, electrical, plumbing/sanitary, mechanical, electronic, and communication works, prepared by the architect and the respective allied professionals
- Prepares **Technical Specifications** describing the type and quality of materials, finish, manner of construction, and general construction conditions
- Submits **seven (7) sets** of all construction drawings and technical specifications to the owner for the purpose of obtaining a **building permit**
- **Updates the SPPCC** based on any changes in scope, requirements, or market conditions
- Assists the owner in filing required documents to secure approval from **government authorities having jurisdiction** over the project design

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: The completion of the Contract Document Phase represents **90% of the architect's total work**. If the owner fails to implement the plans and documents for construction after this phase, the architect is entitled to receive compensation equivleant to **90% of the agreed architect's fee**.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### Phase 5: Bidding or Negotiation Phase

In this phase, the architect:

- **Prepares the Bid Documents** — forms for contract letting, documents for construction, invitation/instruction to bidders, forms for bidders' proposals, general/specific conditions of contract, etc.
- **Assists the owner** from the early stage of establishing a list of prospective contractors to awarding the construction contract

**For competitive bids/procurements**, the architect:
- Furnishes complete sets of Bid Documents in as many sets as required (loaned to bidders at a cost covering direct and indirect costs of preparation, packaging, reproduction, and delivery)
- Helps organize and conduct **pre-bid conferences**
- Responds to questions from bidders
- Assists the owner in obtaining proposals from contractors, analyzes bid results, and prepares abstract of bids, **Notice of Award**, Notice to Proceed, and other construction contracts

**For negotiated contracts**, the architect performs similar functions but negotiates with **one contractor** instead of many bidders.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: All Bid Documents are the **intellectual property of the Architect** under Sec. 33 of R.A. No. 9266. Bidders must return bid documents, and must not reproduce or use them for unauthorized purposes. The owner likewise must not use the documents for any purpose other than the specific project under agreement.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### Phase 6: Construction Phase

During construction, the architect:

- **Makes decisions** on all claims of the owner and contractors on all matters relating to the execution and progress of work, or the interpretation of the Contract Documents
- **Prepares change orders**, gathers, and turns over to the owner written guarantees required of the contractor and sub-contractors
- **Makes periodic visits** to the project site to familiarize with general progress and quality of work and to ascertain that work proceeds in accordance with the Contract Documents
- **Determines the amount owing** to the contractor and issues corresponding **Certificates for Payment** based on observations and the Contractor's Applications for Payment
- Conducts the necessary inspection to determine the date of **substantial and final completion** and issues the **final Certificate for Payment**

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="note"
- Text: The architect is **not required to make exhaustive or continuous 8-hour on-site supervision** to check the quality of work. The architect shall not be held responsible for the contractor's failure to carry out construction work in accordance with the Contract Documents.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


If the owner requires full-time (8-hour) construction supervision, a **separate full-time supervisor** shall be hired and agreed upon under the conditions of **SPP Document 204-A (Fulltime Supervision Services)**.

***

## The Six Phases at a Glance

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Phase | Key Activities | Primary Output | |---|---|---| | **1. Project Definition** | Consultation, data gathering, program review | Initial SPPCC, Architectural Program | | **2. Schematic Design** | Conceptual line drawings, budget/site evaluation | Schematic Plans, updated SPPCC | | **3. Design Development** | Plans, elevations, sections, outline specs | DD Documents, updated SPPCC | | **4. Contract Documents** | Full construction drawings + technical specs | 7-set permit drawings, updated S
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## Manner of Providing Services

The architect may enter into contract with the owner as **Lead Professional** in two ways:

1. **Single Contract** — One contract between the architect and owner, with separate sub-consultancy contracts between the architect and other allied professionals (engineers, etc.). Professional responsibilities and civil liabilities of each licensed professional remain separate; the architect does not assume the responsibilities of the engineers.

2. **Separate Contracts** — The architect and the engineering/allied professionals each execute separate contracts directly with the owner. Again, professional responsibilities remain separate and distinct.

***

## Project Classification Groups

Professional architectural work is classified according to the **degree of complexity and creative skill required**. These groupings determine the corresponding scale of charges (minimum basic fee) in the Architect's Guidelines.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Group | Description | Typical Building Types | |---|---|---| | **Group 1** | Buildings of the simplest utilization and character | Armories, bakeries, freight facilities, hangars, industrial plants, manufacturing plants, warehouses, parking structures, public markets, service garages | | **Group 2** | Buildings of moderate complexity of plan/design | Art galleries, banks, call centers, churches, colleges, dormitories, exhibition halls, libraries, malls, motels, nursing homes, office buildings,
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## Minimum Basic Fee Schedule

The architect's fee for Regular Design Services is primarily computed as a **Percentage (%) of Project Construction Cost (PCC)**, with the specific rates detailed in the Architect's Guidelines.

### Groups 1–3 (Fee scales by PCC Range)

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


### Groups 4–9 (Fixed or Special Rate Structures)

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:

- Text: | Group | Fee Basis | |---|---| | **Group 4** (Residences) | **10%** of Project Construction Cost (flat) | | **Group 5** (Monumental) | 10% of PCC (requires consummate design skill and precise detailing) | | **Group 6** (Repetitive) | 1st structure: full basic fee; 2nd: 80% of basic fee; 3rd: 60%; succeeding: 40% | | **Group 7** (Housing Projects) | 1st unit: 10% of PCC; 2nd–10th: fee of 1st + 60% of basic fee per additional unit; 11th+: fee of 10 units + 30% of basic fee per additional unit | |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## What Is Included in the Project Construction Cost (PCC)?

The PCC — the basis of fee computation — means the **cost of the completed building to the owner**, including:

- Structure
- Plumbing/sanitary and electrical fixtures
- Mechanical equipment, elevators, escalators, air-conditioning systems
- Fire protection systems, alarm and clock systems
- Communications and electronic systems
- All elements attached to the building and all items indicated in the plans, designs, drawings, and specifications prepared by the architect and consultants
- Architectural interiors (AI), site development plan elements, and other items additionally planned/designed by the architect

The PCC **does not include** any professional fees (architect, engineers, specialist consultants) or salaries of construction inspectors. If materials are furnished by the owner below market cost, the PCC is nonetheless computed based on **current fair market value costs**.

The broader **Project Development Cost** includes PCC plus all professional fees, permits, clearances, utilities, cost of acquiring the site, and cost of money.

***

## Methods of Compensation

Five methods of compensation apply to Regular Design Services:

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0010 component="ComparisonTable" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: | Method | Best Used For | Key Feature | |---|---|---| | **Percentage of PCC** | All regular building projects (Groups 1–9) | Most common; fee tied to construction cost | | **MDPE (Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses)** | Non-creative tasks (research, reports, data gathering) | Multiplier of 1.5–2.5 on direct personnel hours | | **Professional Fee + Expenses** | Continuing/repeat relationships | Fixed sum + reimbursements | | **Lump Sum / Fixed Fee** | Government projects; well-defined scope |
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]


***

## Owner's Responsibilities

Under SPP 202, the owner's obligations are equally important to the architect's services:

1. **Provide full information** about project requirements
2. **Designate a representative** authorized to act on the owner's behalf
3. **Promptly examine and render decisions** on documents submitted by the architect, to avoid unreasonable delays — all orders to the General Contractor must be issued **through the Architect**
4. **Furnish or direct the architect** to obtain (at the owner's expense) a certified site survey covering topography, utilities, zoning, deed restrictions, soil investigations, borings, and test pits
5. **Promptly pay** for architectural and all engineering/allied services required for the project
6. **Pay separately** for acoustic, communication, electronic, and other specialty system design services
7. **Arrange and pay** for legal, auditing, insurance, and other ancillary services
8. **Pay for all reimbursable expenses** and all applicable taxes (exclusive of income tax) imposed on the architect as a result of services rendered
9. **Notify the architect promptly** in writing if anything is observed that may impair the successful implementation of the project

***

## Other Conditions on Services

### Fee When Construction Is Not Implemented

The Contract Documents Phase equals **90% of the architect's work**. If the owner fails to implement the plans for construction, the architect is entitled to **90% of the agreed fee**.

### Changes Ordered by the Owner

If the architect renders additional professional services due to **changes ordered by the owner** after approval of outputs, the owner shall pay the architect for extra time, resources, drafting, or other office expenses.

### Suspension or Abandonment of Work

If work is abandoned or suspended in whole or in part, the owner shall pay the architect for **services rendered up to the point of suspension or abandonment**.

### Different Periods of Construction

If portions of the building are erected at different times, construction phase fees shall be **adjusted proportionately**. If the suspension of construction **exceeds six (6) months**, the fee for remaining works shall be **doubled**.

### Per Diem and Travel Expenses

A per diem plus traveling and living expenses are chargeable to the owner whenever the architect or authorized representative must perform services at a locality **beyond 50 km (radial distance)** from the architect's established office.

### Specialist Consultants

If the owner requires specialist consultants (acoustic, illumination, etc.), they are engaged with the architect's consent, paid separately by the owner, and their cost shall **not be deducted from the architect's fee**. A **coordination fee** is payable to the architect for coordinating these specialists.

### scale Models, 3D Models, and Walk-Thru Presentations

Should scale models or 3D/walk-thru presentations be required, costs are paid separately by the owner and are subject to a **coordination fee** payable to the architect.

### Ownership of Documents

All designs, drawings, models, specifications, and contract documents — whether the work was ultimately executed or not — are the **intellectual property and documents of the Architect** under Sec. 33 of R.A. No. 9266. They are not to be reproduced or used on other work without a written agreement with the architect.

### Government Taxes

The architect's fee is a **net amount**. Any tax (exclusive of income tax) that the national or local government imposes on the architect as a result of services rendered shall be paid by the **owner**.

### Signboard Design

All signboards placed at the project site during construction must be **approved by the architect** as to size, design, and contents. After completion, the owner or building lessee shall consult the architect for the design and size of all signboards, directories, and display boards placed on exterior or public areas of the building.

***

## Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**
- Always obtain the **owner's written approval** at the end of each phase before proceeding to the next — approvals at the Schematic and Design Development phases are critical to protect the architect if design directions change later.
- The 90% rule is a key protection: ensure the owner-architect agreement explicitly states the fee owing at the Contract Documents Phase to avoid disputes when projects are shelved post-documentation.
- Periodic site visits during the Construction Phase are an obligation, but **full-time 8-hour supervision is a separate service** under SPP 204-A and must be separately contracted and compensated.
- Bid documents are the architect's intellectual property — require a bond or deposit from bidders to ensure their return.

**For Clients / Project Proponents:**
- All orders to the General Contractor **must flow through the architect** — bypassing the architect undermines the construction contract and can expose the owner to legal liability for any resulting defects.
- The architect's fee is a **net amount** — factor in VAT and other applicable taxes (to be shouldered by the owner) when budgeting professional fees.
- Cost estimates (SPPCC) at any stage are professional opinions, not guarantees. Competitive bidding results may deviate from estimates.
- For Group 9 (alterations/renovations), the minimum basic fee is **150% of the applicable Group 1–5 rate** — not a flat rate — reflecting the greater complexity and risk involved in working with existing structures.

***

## Relationship to Other SPP Documents

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---



---

## Exam Tip

LEA Swipe: SPP 202 five phases and fee percentages: SD (Phase 1) = 15% of basic fee | DD (Phase 2) = 20% | CD (Phase 3) = 30% (largest single phase) | Bidding (Phase 4) = 5% (smallest) | CA (Phase 5) = 30%. The 15-20-30-5-30 percentage sequence is the most tested fee allocation on the exam.

# SPP Document 205: Standards of Professional Practice on Post-Construction Services


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the exam task in one sentence: what is being classified, measured, approved, or restricted? Then identify the controlling rule named by the item and avoid importing requirements from a different law, table, or occupancy condition.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **SPP Document 205: Standards of Professional Practice on Post-Construction Services** as enough to answer. In LEA-style questions, first anchor the question to the exact code, scope, and condition being tested, then choose the option that follows that rule.

**Retrieval prompt:** What fact in the question tells you which rule set applies, and what option would become wrong if the scope changed?

## Overview

**SPP Document 205** governs **Post-Construction Services** — the professional architectural services rendered after a building has been constructed and turned over to the owner. It replaces the earlier **1979 UAP Doc. 205** and forms part of the Supplemental Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of **Republic Act No. 9266** (The Architecture Act of 2004).

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Identify the scope of SPP Doc 205 Post-Construction Services: building start-up and commissioning, preparation of record (as-built) drawings, post-occupancy evaluation, facility management support, and maintenance and operation manuals (MOMM); distinguish post-construction services from construction administration under SPP 202; apply the per-diem or fixed-fee compensation basis.
---
SPP 205 is strategically placed as the **final document in the core services sequence** (SPP 201 through 205), and together with SPP 206 (Comprehensive Architectural Services), it represents the full lifecycle of architectural involvement from project inception through the productive life of the built structure. Post-construction services are what give full meaning to what the profession calls **Comprehensive Architectural Services** — they close the loop between design intent and long-term building performance.

***

## Introduction and Policy rationale

### 1.1 Beyond Maintenance and Upkeep

Building administration and management **goes beyond maintenance and upkeep functions**. It requires the services of a **multi-disciplinary professional** who can perform a wide range of functions for the efficient and economical operation and maintenance of a building, facility, or complex. An architect — trained to coordinate structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, interiors, and site systems — is uniquely suited for this role.

### 1.2 Keeping Communications Open

A defining feature of post-construction services is the maintenance of **multi-party communication channels**. Specifically, SPP 205 keeps channels open among:

- Building owners and operators
- Architects and engineers (designers)
- Builders and contractors (constructors)
- Manufacturers and suppliers (material and product vendors)
- Building research groups (technical knowledge sources)
- Utility providers
- Furniture and equipment vendors
- Building administrators and property managers

This continuous communication network ensures that information on building performance and upkeep remains accessible to all stakeholders throughout the building's operational life.

### 1.3 The Architect's Role: Building Administrator and/or Property Manager

The **Architect may be engaged as the Building Administrator and/or Property Manager** of a commercial, industrial, residential, or institutional building, facility, or complex. The primary objective of this engagement is to **maximize the lifespan of the building** in order to **produce the maximum economic return** for the owner. This positions SPP 205 not merely as a maintenance document but as a strategic asset management framework — the architect's mandate is to protect and grow the value of the built asset over time.

***

## Scope of Services

The SPP 205 scope of services is organized into two principal clusters:

1. **Building and Facilities Administration** (Section 2.1) — active, ongoing management of the building's physical and operational condition
2. **Post-Construction Evaluation** (Section 2.2) — retrospective assessment of the building's performance relative to design intent

***

### 2.1 Building and Facilities Administration

Building and Facilities Administration encompasses four sub-services that together constitute the full operational management mandate of the architect as Building Administrator.

#### 2.1.1 Building Maintenance

The Architect shall:

- **See to it that the building and all its parts** — structure, plumbing, electrical, partitions, finishes, etc. — are all in good condition
- **Formulate and enforce rules** for the proper use of the building and facility, particularly in the common areas and the emergency/egress/exit areas
- **Monitor security services** — ensuring adequate security coverage for the property and its occupants
- **Monitor maintenance and upkeep services** — cleanliness of corridors, lobbies, stairs and other common areas, exits, parking areas, and garbage collection

Building Maintenance is the foundational layer of post-construction service — it ensures that the physical asset remains safe, functional, and presentable for occupants and visitors.

#### 2.1.2 Grounds and Landscaping Supervision

The Architect shall:

- **Supervise landscape contractors and gardeners** for the proper watering, pruning, trimming, and maintenance of the landscape (both hardscapes and softscapes)
- **Maintain orderly entrances, exits, and parking areas** — ensuring vehicular and pedestrian circulation is functional and safe
- **Maintain streets and road rights-of-way (RROWs), walkways, and ramps** — keeping all outdoor circulation routes in compliance with accessibility and safety standards

Grounds and Landscaping Supervision reflects the architect's understanding that a building's value is inseparable from the quality of its surrounding environment.

#### 2.1.3 Building Equipment Maintenance

The Architect shall:

- **Assist the proper third parties** in seeing to it that all building equipment — air-conditioning systems, sprinkler systems, generators, transformers, telecommunications equipment, and other installed systems — are **properly maintained and in good working condition**

The use of "assist the proper third parties" is deliberate: the architect does not personally service or repair technical equipment (which requires separate licensed trades), but **coordinates and monitors** the activities of specialist service contractors to ensure that equipment is maintained per manufacturers' specifications and building code requirements.

#### 2.1.4 Business Development and Management

The Architect shall:

- **Innovate schemes to attain maximum building occupancy** — developing and implementing tenant attraction and retention strategies to optimize the building's revenue-generating capacity
- **Bill the tenants for rentals and utilities** — including electricity, water, telephone, cable, gas, and other related dues and maintenance charges

Business Development and Management is the most commercially oriented sub-service under SPP 205. It positions the Architect as a property manager in the full business sense — responsible not only for physical upkeep but also for **financial performance and occupancy optimization** of the building portfolio.

***

### Building and Facilities Administration: Services at a Glance

***

### 2.2 Post-Construction Evaluation

The **Post-Construction Evaluation** cluster is triggered **upon the request of the Owner** — it is not a routine ongoing function like Building and Facilities Administration, but a specific analytical engagement initiated at the owner's direction.

The Architect shall:

**a. Evaluate the initial design program vs. the actual use of the facility**
Assesses whether the spaces, systems, and infrastructure originally designed for the building are being used as intended — identifying programmatic mismatches that may require modifications (e.g., under-utilized spaces, overloaded systems, or informal space repurposing by occupants).

**b. Determine the effectiveness of the various building systems and the materials systems in use**
Evaluates how well the structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and envelope systems are performing relative to design specifications and occupant expectations — including energy performance, maintenance costs, and system reliability.

**c. Assist the proper third parties in evaluating the functional effectiveness of the design and construction process undertaken**
Facilitates multi-party reviews by involving the original designers, engineers, contractors, and specialist consultants in a structured assessment of the entire design and construction process — identifying best practices and lessons learned for future projects.

**d. Study, research, and give solutions to any discovered/emerging/evolving defects and failures**
Addresses defects such as shrinkage, water seepage, spalling, settlement, and other building pathologies that emerge during the building's operational life. This is **explicitly referred to in SPP 205 as "forensic investigation" of the building's systems**, with a cross-reference to **SPP 203.13 (Forensic Architecture)**.

If the post-construction evaluation under SPP 205 reveals defects that require deeper forensic investigation — particularly those that may involve contractor or designer liability — the owner should engage a Consulting Architect under SPP 203.13.

***

## Manner of Providing Services

As with other SPP documents, the Architect under SPP 205 may enter into contract with the Owner in **two possible ways**:

### 3.1 Dual Capacity: Architect-of-Record + Consulting Architect for Post-Construction Services

The original **Architect-of-Record (Aor)** who designed and supervised the building assumes the additional role of **Building Administrator and/or Property Manager**. This arrangement offers several advantages:

- The Aor has **intimate knowledge of the design intent**, construction details, and building systems — making defect identification and performance evaluation significantly more effective
- Communication between the operational and design phases is seamless, reducing the risk of misinterpretation
- The owner benefits from **continuity of professional relationship** throughout the full project lifecycle

### 3.2 Consulting Architect for Post-Construction Services Only

A **separate Consulting Architect (CA)** is retained solely for post-construction services, independent of the original design team. This may be preferable when:

- The original Aor is no longer available or no longer engaged
- The owner requires an **independent, objective assessment** of the building's performance (especially relevant for post-construction evaluations that may reveal design or construction deficiencies)
- The building was designed by an in-house team or a foreign architect not eligible to practice in the Philippines

***

## Method of Compensation

### The Incentive Logic of the Percentage Method

The percentage-of-gross-rentals method is notable because it **aligns the Architect's financial interest with the Owner's asset performance**:

- If the Architect successfully innovates schemes to increase building occupancy (2.1.4 Business Development), gross rentals increase — and so does the Architect's fee
- Conversely, poor building administration that drives tenants away reduces rentals and reduces the Architect's fee
- This creates a **performance-based compensation structure** that incentivizes proactive, high-quality building management
- The owner also separately pays **repair and maintenance expenses** — the 4–6% fee covers the Architect's professional service, not the cost of physical works

***

## SPP 205 and the Comprehensive Architectural Services Continuum

SPP 205 is the **final link in the SPP 201–205 service chain**, which together constitute the full scope of **Comprehensive Architectural Services (CAS)** as defined under SPP 206:

## Relationship to Other SPP Documents

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

***

## Practical Notes for Architects and Clients

**For Architects:**

- The **Architect as Building Administrator** is a distinct professional engagement from the Architect as designer — it requires a separate service agreement, clearly defined scope, and separate compensation. Do not conflate post-construction services with the warranty obligations that flow from the design contract.
- The **forensic investigation cross-reference** to SPP 203 is a practical reminder: when post-construction evaluation reveals systemic defects (especially those suggesting design or construction negligence), a specialist Forensic Architect under SPP 203.13 should be engaged — both to protect the owner's legal position and to protect the building administrator from being perceived as covering up findings.
- Under the **percentage-of-gross-rentals** compensation model, the Architect's business development mandate (2.1.4) is not optional — it is a core deliverable. Architects taking on SPP 205 engagements should have competence in leasing strategy, tenant relations, and facilities financial management, or should partner with qualified property managers.

**For Clients / Building Owners:**

- Engaging the **original Architect-of-Record** under SPP 205 (dual capacity) is generally the most cost-effective option for the first 5–10 years after turnover — the Aor's intimate knowledge of the building's design and construction significantly reduces the time and cost of diagnosing operational issues.
- The **4–6% of gross rentals** fee structure means that for large commercial buildings with high rental income, the monthly Architect's fee can be substantial — owners should evaluate whether the Architect's full Building Administrator scope justifies this rate versus a more limited consulting retainer under PFPE or MDPE.
- Post-construction evaluation (Section 2.2) should be scheduled **systematically** — ideally at 1 year, 3 years, and 5 years post-turnover — rather than only triggered by visible defects. Early evaluations catch system failures before they become costly, and provide structured feedback to the design team for future projects.
